Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: To find out whether a person has taken too much acetaminophen and to monitor how well overdose treatment is working.
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: This blood test measures the amount of acetaminophen in the blood. A high level suggests overdose or toxicity and may indicate risk for serious liver damage, sometimes requiring immediate treatment and repeat testing to confirm levels are falling.

aliases: Cut down Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener (CAGE) tool
Tolerance, Annoyed Cut down, Eye-opener (T-ACE) tool
Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: Questionnaires used to check for unhealthy alcohol use, assess risk for alcohol use disorder (AUD), and in some cases help determine whether AUD is mild, moderate, or severe.
associated_symptoms: Drinking more or longer than you planned
Trying to cut down or quit but being unable to do it
Hiding liquor bottles and glasses so others don't see evidence of drinking
Continuing to drink even if it causes problems in your personal relationships, work, school, and/or health
Building up a tolerance to alcohol
Using alcohol when it's not safe, such as driving
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: Alcohol use screening tests are questionnaires that help identify unhealthy alcohol use and possible AUD. Results may show whether a person is at risk for AUD or indicate severity, ranging from mild to severe. A positive screen can guide counseling, treatment planning, support groups, and medicines.

Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: To detect alcohol in the blood and estimate how much it is affecting a person, including for legal, employment, alcohol poisoning, and alcohol use disorder monitoring purposes.
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: This test measures ethanol in blood and is commonly reported as BAC. Results help assess recent alcohol use and the degree of impairment, with higher BAC levels causing greater intoxication and potentially life-threatening effects such as coma, respiratory problems, or death. A blood alcohol test can usually detect alcohol for up to about 12 hours after the last drink, and interpretation can be influenced by timing and personal factors such as weight, age, sex, drinking rate, food intake, medicines, and alcohol tolerance.

Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: Used to determine whether a person has been exposed to certain heavy metals and how much of the metal is in the body.
associated_symptoms: Tingling in the hands and feet
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: Higher-than-normal blood levels of a heavy metal may suggest heavy metal poisoning, though normal or low levels do not always rule it out because some metals leave the bloodstream quickly and are stored in tissues. Results may guide further testing and, in some cases, treatment such as chelation therapy to help remove the metal from the body.

Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: Opioid testing is used to detect opioids in urine, blood, saliva, sweat, or hair. It may be used for therapeutic drug monitoring, to check that prescribed opioids are being taken appropriately, to look for unprescribed opioid use or misuse, and as part of broader drug testing for employment, legal, treatment, or sports purposes.
associated_symptoms: Complaining of increasing pain even though the condition isn't getting worse
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: Opioid testing shows whether opioids are present in a sample, but it does not by itself diagnose misuse or opioid use disorder. Screening tests may need confirmation because false positives can occur, and results can be affected by the body’s metabolism, other medicines, and the testing method used.

Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: Measures the amount of salicylates in the blood. It is used to help diagnose acute or chronic aspirin or other salicylate poisoning and to monitor people taking prescription-strength aspirin for arthritis or other inflammatory conditions.
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: A salicylates level test checks blood salicylate concentration. High levels suggest possible aspirin or other salicylate poisoning and may require immediate treatment; results are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, and other blood tests.

Toxicology/Drug Level.purpose: This test detects tricyclic antidepressants in blood or urine and may measure the amount present. It is used to help guide TCA dosing, identify misuse, and diagnose a TCA overdose.
Toxicology/Drug Level.summary: A TCA screen shows whether tricyclic antidepressants are present in blood or urine and, in some tests, how much is present. Blood results reflect bloodstream levels and may lead to dosage adjustment; urine tests may be qualitative or quantitative. Dangerously high levels require immediate treatment.

aliases: Acid-Fast Bacillus Smear and Culture and Sensitivity
Mycobacterium tuberculosis Nucleic Acid Amplification Test
Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To diagnose active tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections, especially after a positive TB screening test or abnormal chest x-ray, and to help determine whether treatment is working and which antibiotic is most effective.
associated_symptoms: Cough that lasts for three weeks or more
Microbiology/Infection.summary: AFB smear, culture, molecular (NAAT), and susceptibility testing look for acid-fast bacteria in sputum or sometimes skin/nerve tissue. A positive smear suggests infection but usually needs culture confirmation, while a positive culture confirms active TB or another mycobacterial infection. NAAT can detect TB more quickly and may show rifampicin resistance, and susceptibility testing helps choose the most effective antibiotic.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether a bacterial infection is present and, if so, identify the type of bacteria causing it so the best treatment can be chosen. It is used to help diagnose infections from different sample sites such as the throat, urine, sputum, blood, stool, and wounds.
related_diseases_or_conditions: bacterial or fungal infections in the respiratory tract
bacterial or fungal infections in the blood
bacterial infections in the digestive system
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A bacteria culture test grows bacteria from a sample in the lab to identify the organism causing an infection. A positive result usually means a bacterial infection is present, and further testing such as antibiotic sensitivity testing may be done to choose the most effective medicine. Results often take one to several days because the bacteria must grow enough to be identified.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether bacterial vaginosis is the cause of symptoms that appear to be from a vaginal infection.
associated_symptoms: unusual vaginal discharge that can be gray or white
strong fish-like odor, especially after sex
itching around the outside of the vagina
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A bacterial vaginosis test examines vaginal discharge for signs of BV using methods such as microscopy, odor testing, vaginal pH, or PCR. Abnormal smear or whiff test results suggest a bacterial infection, while a pH above 4.5 makes BV more likely but does not diagnose it alone. If BV is found, treatment is usually with antibiotics, and recurrence can happen after treatment.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) is causing diarrhea or other symptoms of infection by testing a stool sample for C. diff toxins, toxin genes, or GDH antigens, often alongside tests for other causes of diarrhea.
associated_symptoms: Watery diarrhea three or more times a day with no other known cause
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive result may indicate C. diff toxin or toxin genes are present and causing illness, while a negative result generally means no signs of infection were found. However, a toxin test alone can miss infection if toxins break down, so results are often interpreted with other C. diff tests, symptoms, and medical history.

aliases: serum varicella immunoglobulin G antibody level
Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To check whether a person has a current or past varicella zoster virus (VZV) infection, to help confirm chickenpox or shingles, and sometimes to check for immunity to VZV.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: Chickenpox and shingles tests look for VZV itself or VZV antibodies in blood or blister fluid. A positive result in a symptomatic person suggests chickenpox or shingles, while antibodies without symptoms usually mean past infection or vaccination. Results may also be used to assess immunity, especially in people at higher risk of complications.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: A chlamydia test is used to check for chlamydia infection in people who may have no symptoms or who have symptoms of infection, and to help diagnose or rule out chlamydia so treatment can begin early and prevent spread and complications.
associated_symptoms: unusual fluid discharge from your genitals
unusual fluid discharge from your rectum
pain in one or both testicles
swelling in one or both testicles
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative result means chlamydia was not present when the sample was collected. A positive result means infection with chlamydia, which should be treated with antibiotics, partners should be notified, and retesting is recommended about 3 months after treatment because repeat infection is common.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To help diagnose a current, reactivated, or past CMV infection in people at risk for complications, including people with weakened immune systems, transplant recipients, pregnant people with symptoms, and newborns with signs of infection.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: CMV tests look for signs of cytomegalovirus in blood, sputum, cerebrospinal fluid, tissue, amniotic fluid, saliva, or urine. The results can show whether a person has ever been infected, but they cannot by themselves distinguish a current, past, or reactivated infection. In people at risk, additional testing may be needed to confirm diagnosis and guide treatment.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether a person has a dengue virus infection, especially when they have symptoms after recent travel to or exposure in an area where dengue is common.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: The test is usually a blood test that may use either molecular methods (such as PCR) or antibody testing. PCR is most accurate early in illness, while antibody tests are more useful after several days. A positive result suggests dengue infection, while a negative result does not always rule it out, especially if testing is done too early or too late; follow-up testing may be needed.

aliases: Type A and B Antigen Detection
Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to determine whether influenza A or influenza B is causing respiratory symptoms, help guide treatment decisions such as whether antiviral medicine is appropriate, and support monitoring of flu and COVID-19 outbreaks in the community. Some versions also test for other respiratory viruses or bird flu.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Diseases that weaken the immune system
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive result means influenza A or B was found and you most likely have the seasonal flu; a negative result does not fully rule out flu, especially after a rapid antigen test, and more testing may be needed if symptoms continue. Molecular tests are more accurate than rapid antigen tests, and combination tests can identify other respiratory viruses at the same time.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to find out whether a fungus is causing an infection, identify the type of fungus, help choose the best treatment, and check whether treatment is working.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A fungal culture grows a sample in the lab to look for fungi. A positive result means fungi were found and usually identifies the specific fungus causing the infection; a negative result means no fungi were found and another cause is more likely.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to screen for gonorrhea in people without symptoms who may have been exposed, and to diagnose or rule out gonorrhea in people with symptoms. It is often done together with chlamydia testing and may also be paired with testing for syphilis and/or HIV.
associated_symptoms: An unusual discharge from the genitals
Pain in the testicles or scrotum
Tenderness in the testicles or scrotum
Swelling in the testicles or scrotum
A pus-like fluid that drains from one or both eyes
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative result means gonorrhea was not found, but testing may be too early after exposure to detect the infection. A positive result means gonorrhea infection is present and requires prompt antibiotic treatment, partner notification, and follow-up testing to confirm cure.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to check for a bacterial infection and determine whether the bacteria are Gram-positive or Gram-negative; it may also be used to help diagnose fungal infections and guide further testing and treatment.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A Gram stain examines a sample for bacteria and shows whether they stain purple (Gram-positive) or pink/red (Gram-negative), along with their shape, which helps identify the likely cause of infection and choose effective antibiotics. If no bacteria are seen, infection is less likely, though the sample may have too few organisms; the test can also suggest fungal infection but cannot detect viruses.

aliases: HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibody and antigen evaluation
human immunodeficiency virus antibody test, type 1
Microbiology/Infection.purpose: An HIV screening test is used to determine whether a person has been infected with HIV, either as part of routine screening or after a possible exposure, so treatment can begin early and transmission to others can be reduced.
associated_symptoms: Flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills, aches
Swollen lymph nodes (in your neck, groin, or armpit)
Microbiology/Infection.summary: HIV screening tests look for HIV antibodies, antigens, or viral RNA in blood, saliva, or urine depending on the test type. A negative result may be too early to rule out infection if exposure was recent, while a positive screening result usually requires follow-up confirmation unless a NAT was done. Early detection helps patients start antiretroviral therapy and avoid progressing to AIDS or spreading HIV.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To measure the amount of HIV genetic material in the blood, mainly to guide HIV treatment, check how well antiretroviral therapy is working, monitor changes in infection over time, and in some cases help diagnose HIV or test newborns exposed to HIV.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: An HIV viral load test shows how much HIV is in the blood. An undetectable or low result usually means treatment is working and the infection is under control, while a high result suggests the virus is growing and treatment may need to be changed. When used for diagnosis, any detected HIV generally indicates infection, and follow-up testing such as a CD4 count may be ordered.

aliases: rapid urease test (RUT) for H. pylori
Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether an H. pylori infection is causing digestive symptoms and to confirm whether treatment has cured the infection.
associated_symptoms: Feeling full too soon while eating a meal
Red blood in vomit or vomit that looks like coffee grounds
Sudden, sharp or severe belly pain that doesn't go away
Worsening symptoms if you already know you have an ulcer
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive H. pylori test means the bacteria are present and treatment with antibiotics is usually needed; repeat testing may be done after treatment to confirm the infection is gone. A negative result usually means H. pylori is unlikely, though other causes of symptoms may need to be evaluated.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To check blood for signs of a current or past viral hepatitis infection; it is also used to help determine whether hepatitis A, B, D, or E is present now or in the past, and to guide follow-up testing for active versus acute or chronic infection.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative result usually means hepatitis is unlikely, while a positive or abnormal result suggests hepatitis antigens or antibodies were found in the blood. Abnormal results may indicate an active infection now or a past infection that cleared, and follow-up tests are often needed to determine whether the infection is acute or chronic.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether a person has a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection. Depending on whether sores are present, the test may use fluid from a sore for viral culture or PCR, or blood to look for HSV antibodies.
associated_symptoms: Blisters or sores on the mouth
Blisters or sores on the genitals
Blisters or sores on the anus
Blisters or sores on the buttocks
Blisters or sores on other areas of skin
Pain or tingling in the affected area
related_diseases_or_conditions: Infection in a baby during childbirth
Microbiology/Infection.summary: Negative results usually mean HSV was not found, though blood antibody tests can be falsely negative if done too soon after infection. Positive results mean HSV signs were found; if antibodies are detected in blood, this may reflect a current or past infection. Results should be interpreted with symptoms and history.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Screens for high-risk HPV infection that can cause cervical precancer and cervical cancer by testing a sample of cervical cells; it may also be used with a Pap test (cotesting) and, in some cases, to help guide treatment decisions for oropharyngeal (throat) cancer using biopsy tissue.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative HPV test means high-risk HPV was not found. A positive result means high-risk HPV DNA was found, indicating infection and a higher future risk of cervical precancer or cancer, but not necessarily current cancer. Follow-up may include colposcopy and/or more frequent HPV or HPV/Pap testing.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Measures the amount of immunoglobulins (antibodies) in the blood, usually IgM, IgG, and IgA, to help diagnose conditions that affect the immune system and to evaluate abnormal low or high immunoglobulin levels.
associated_symptoms: repeated infections from the same germ
serious infections from germs that don't usually cause problems in healthy people
yeast infection in the mouth, eyes, or digestive tract
related_diseases_or_conditions: cancers affecting the bone marrow, blood, or immune system
infections a baby may be born with
Microbiology/Infection.summary: The test compares IgM, IgG, and IgA levels. Low levels may suggest reduced protein, impaired immunoglobulin production, or immunodeficiency, while high levels may be seen with autoimmune disease, infection, liver disease, or certain cancers. The test alone cannot diagnose a condition, so abnormal results usually require further testing.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Measures lactate (lactic acid) in blood, and sometimes cerebrospinal fluid, to help diagnose and monitor lactic acidosis and other conditions that raise lactate; it may also help evaluate meningitis and distinguish bacterial from viral infection when CSF is tested.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A lactate test shows whether lactate is abnormally high, but it cannot identify the cause by itself. Mild to moderate elevation is called hyperlactatemia, while higher persistent elevation with acidic blood indicates lactic acidosis, which is more serious and needs prompt treatment. When cerebrospinal fluid is tested, high lactate suggests bacterial meningitis, while normal or slightly high lactate suggests viral meningitis.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to determine whether a person has Legionnaires' disease by detecting Legionella bacteria in urine, sputum, and sometimes lung tissue; a blood test may help show exposure but cannot diagnose infection.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive result probably means Legionnaires' disease. A negative result may mean another infection or that too few Legionella bacteria were present in the sample. Providers may use symptoms, history, and other tests such as chest x-ray or culture to confirm the diagnosis.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To find out whether a person has a Lyme disease infection, usually after exposure or possible exposure to infected ticks and when symptoms suggest Lyme disease.
associated_symptoms: A reddish, round skin rash that slowly gets bigger over several days
Rashes on other parts of your body
Pain that comes and goes in your muscles, joints, bones, and tendons
Tingling in your hands or feet
Microbiology/Infection.summary: Lyme disease tests usually measure antibodies in blood, and sometimes cerebrospinal fluid, to help diagnose Lyme disease. A negative early blood test can be falsely negative, while a positive blood test may need confirmation with a second test. CSF testing can help show whether the infection has spread to the nervous system, but results alone do not diagnose the disease.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To find out if a person has a MRSA infection and, in some cases, to see whether treatment for a MRSA infection is working.
associated_symptoms: red, swollen bumps on the skin
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive MRSA test means MRSA bacteria were found and the person has a MRSA infection. Results are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, and other tests. Mild skin infections may be treated by cleaning, draining, and covering the wound and using topical or oral antibiotics, while more serious infections may require IV antibiotics in the hospital.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To diagnose malaria by detecting malaria parasites or their proteins in blood, identify the type of parasite to guide treatment, and help control spread of the disease.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A malaria test looks for signs of malaria parasites in a blood sample. A positive result means malaria is present and treatment should start right away; a negative result does not always rule it out, so repeat testing may be needed. Blood smear testing can identify the parasite type, while rapid tests give faster results but may not identify the type.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To diagnose a current or recent measles or mumps infection, check whether a person is immune because of vaccination or past infection, and help identify and control outbreaks.
associated_symptoms: rash that starts on the face and spreads to the chest and legs
tiny white spots in the mouth
Microbiology/Infection.summary: Negative results usually mean no measles or mumps was found and, for antibody tests, no immunity. A positive molecular test suggests current infection, a positive IgM suggests current or recent infection, and a positive IgG suggests immunity from vaccination or past infection.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether a person has meningococcal disease by detecting Neisseria meningitidis in blood or cerebrospinal fluid.
associated_symptoms: Having a soft spot on the skull
Severe aches or pain in the muscles
Severe aches or pain in the joints
Severe aches or pain in the chest
Severe aches or pain in the abdomen
Microbiology/Infection.summary: These tests look for meningococcal bacteria, their genetic material, or their antigens in blood or CSF. A positive result means Neisseria meningitidis was found and meningococcal disease is likely; a negative result means the bacteria were not found. Prompt antibiotic treatment is important if infection is confirmed.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to help diagnose a mono infection, often with the monospot test for quick results and, if needed, EBV antibody testing and other tests to help identify the cause of symptoms and rule out other infections such as strep throat.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive monospot test may indicate mono, while a negative result does not rule it out because false negatives occur; if symptoms continue, EBV antibody testing may be done. EBV antibody results can show whether infection is recent or past, and a negative EBV test suggests symptoms are likely due to another disorder.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: A urinalysis that includes nitrite testing is used to check general health, including the health of the urinary tract and kidneys, and to help check for a urinary tract infection (UTI).
associated_symptoms: Frequent urges to urinate, even when you have little urine in your bladder
Pain or burning when you pee
Microbiology/Infection.summary: Nitrites in urine may indicate a urinary tract infection because some bacteria convert nitrates to nitrites. However, a negative nitrite result does not rule out infection, since some bacteria do not produce nitrites; other urinalysis findings, especially white blood cells, are also considered.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To check a stool sample for intestinal parasites and their eggs to help determine whether parasites are causing intestinal infection symptoms and to see whether treatment is working.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative result means no parasites or eggs were found, though infection may still be present if too few organisms were in the sample. A positive result means intestinal parasites and/or eggs were found, and the report may identify the type and amount present. Treatment depends on the parasite and overall health, and fluid replacement may be needed to prevent dehydration.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: PCR tests are used to diagnose certain infectious diseases, identify certain genetic changes that can cause disease, and detect small amounts of certain cancer cells that may be missed by other tests.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests detect very small amounts of genetic material from a pathogen or abnormal cells in blood, saliva, mucus, or tissue. They work by amplifying DNA, or RNA that is first converted to DNA, making them highly sensitive for early infection and for detecting disease when only tiny amounts of material are present.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To check whether a parainfluenza virus is causing a respiratory illness, especially in people at higher risk for severe disease or when results may help distinguish viral from bacterial infection as part of a respiratory pathogens panel.
associated_symptoms: A long-lasting cough that may sound like a barking in children
Too much mucus in the lungs or airways
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative result means no parainfluenza virus was found, but it does not completely rule out infection. A positive result means you likely have a parainfluenza infection, although PCR can sometimes detect viral material even when you are not sick from it. Results should be interpreted with your provider in the context of symptoms and risk factors.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Tests used to determine whether a person has pneumococcal disease by looking for Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria or its genetic material/antigen in body samples such as blood, urine, sputum, cerebrospinal fluid, or nasal samples.
associated_symptoms: Not eating or drinking as well
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive test means pneumococcus bacteria were found and pneumococcal disease is likely. A negative test means the bacteria were not found and symptoms are more likely due to another cause. Results are interpreted with symptoms, medical history, and sometimes other tests such as chest x-ray, CBC, ESR, or CRP.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Checks a respiratory sample for multiple viruses and bacteria that can cause respiratory tract infections, helping identify the specific pathogen so the most appropriate treatment can be chosen and unnecessary antibiotics avoided.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive result means a specific pathogen was found and may indicate a single infection or a co-infection; a negative result does not rule out infection because the cause may be a pathogen not included on the panel, an improperly collected or insufficient sample, or a nonbacterial/nonviral condition. Results are interpreted with symptoms, medical history, and other tests to guide treatment and possible follow-up testing.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether respiratory syncytial virus is causing moderate to severe respiratory illness, especially in infants, older adults, people with weakened immune systems, and sometimes for public health tracking during RSV season.
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive RSV test suggests an RSV infection, while a negative result does not completely rule it out because the virus may be present in too small an amount to detect. Testing is usually done with a nasal sample using rapid antigen or RT-PCR methods, and results help guide care for patients with more significant symptoms.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to find out if a person has been infected with a sexually transmitted infection (STI) and to help guide treatment and reduce spread of infection.
associated_symptoms: Discharge and/or itching from the penis
Sores or bumps in the genital or rectal area
Blisters or sores in or around the mouth
related_diseases_or_conditions: Herpes infection affecting the brain or spinal cord
Microbiology/Infection.summary: STI tests use blood, urine, swab, or sometimes lumbar puncture samples to diagnose specific infections. Results show whether an STI is present; if positive, treatment and partner notification are important to prevent complications and further spread.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To detect and identify bacteria or fungi causing infections in the lungs or airways, to assess whether a chronic lung illness has worsened or treatment is working, and to help diagnose respiratory conditions such as pneumonia, tuberculosis, and bronchiectasis.
associated_symptoms: Cough which produces a lot of sputum
Chest pain that gets worse when you breathe deeply or cough
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A sputum culture grows organisms from a sputum sample to see whether harmful bacteria or fungi are present. A normal result means no harmful bacteria or fungi were found, while an abnormal result may indicate infection or a flare-up of a chronic lung condition. Results are interpreted with symptoms, history, and other test findings.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To check whether a sore throat or other symptoms are caused by group A streptococcal infection (strep throat) rather than a viral infection, so that strep throat can be treated with antibiotics and complications prevented.
associated_symptoms: A sudden and severe sore throat
White patches or streaks of pus on the tonsils
Tiny, red spots on the roof of the mouth (petechiae)
A rough, red rash that starts on the face and spreads to another part of the body
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A Strep A test detects group A streptococcal infection using a rapid antigen test or throat culture. A positive result means strep throat or another strep A infection is present; a negative result suggests symptoms are more likely due to something other than strep A, often leading to additional testing if suspicion remains.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: A group B strep test checks for group B streptococcus (GBS) bacteria. In pregnancy, it is used for routine prenatal screening to see whether a pregnant person carries GBS so antibiotics can be given during labor to help prevent infection in the baby. It may also be used to test infants who show signs of infection.
associated_symptoms: full of pus or other drainage
being unable to move the affected joint(s)
Microbiology/Infection.summary: The test detects GBS bacteria in pregnant people or infants. In pregnancy, a positive result usually means IV antibiotics are given during labor to lower the risk of passing the bacteria to the baby. In infants, a positive result may prompt antibiotic treatment because GBS can cause serious illness or death.

aliases: Microhemagglutination assay for antibodies to T. pallidum (MHA-TP)
Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To screen for and confirm syphilis infection by detecting antibodies to the syphilis bacterium in blood or, when needed, cerebrospinal fluid; less commonly, to detect the bacteria directly.
related_diseases_or_conditions: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) involvement of the brain and nervous system
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A negative screening test usually means syphilis is unlikely, though early infection can be missed before antibodies develop. A positive screening test requires confirmatory testing. If confirmed, syphilis is typically treated with penicillin or other antibiotics, with better cure rates in early disease and limited ability to reverse late-stage damage.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To diagnose trichomoniasis in people with symptoms, screen women at high risk for infection, and check for reinfection or persistent infection after treatment; it is often ordered with other STI tests because trichomoniasis increases STI risk.
associated_symptoms: redness or soreness around the genitals
clear, white, yellowish, or greenish vaginal discharge with a fishy smell
itching or irritation inside the penis
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A trichomoniasis test looks for the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis, usually from a swab or urine sample. A positive result means trichomoniasis is present and treatment is needed; a negative wet prep result does not always rule it out, so more accurate tests such as NAATs, rapid antigen tests, or culture may be used if suspicion remains.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To determine whether a person has whooping cough (pertussis), especially after exposure or when symptoms suggest infection, so diagnosis and early treatment can help reduce symptom severity and spread.
associated_symptoms: severe coughing fits followed by a high-pitch "whoop" sound
coughing so hard it causes vomiting
feeling very tired after coughing fits
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive culture means whooping cough is present, while a positive PCR suggests genetic material from the bacteria was found and whooping cough is likely. Negative results do not completely rule out infection, especially if the sample was collected too late or after antibiotics. Blood antibody tests are generally not recommended for diagnosis.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: To diagnose yeast infections, using different testing methods depending on where symptoms are located.
associated_symptoms: Itching in the vagina and vulva
Burning in the vagina and vulva
White discharge that looks like cottage cheese
Redness of the vagina and labia
Swelling of the vagina and labia
Rash on the head of the penis that may be painful
White patches on the inside of cheeks
White patches on the roof of the mouth
Cracks at the corners of the mouth
Redness at the corners of the mouth
Pain if the infection is severe
Redness if the infection is severe
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A yeast infection test helps determine whether symptoms are caused by yeast overgrowth. Results may guide antifungal treatment; if the infection is invasive or suspected in blood or organs, additional culture or other testing on blood, fluid, or tissue may be needed.

Microbiology/Infection.purpose: Used to check for a Zika virus infection, especially in pregnant people who have recently traveled to or had sexual exposure related to an area where Zika risk exists.
associated_symptoms: Red eyes (pink eye, also called conjunctivitis)
Microbiology/Infection.summary: A positive result means a Zika infection is likely. A negative result may mean no infection or that testing was done too early; repeat testing may be needed if exposure is suspected. In pregnancy, a diagnosis can help guide monitoring and preparation for possible fetal or newborn health problems.

Endocrine.purpose: A 17-OHP test is used to help detect and monitor congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), especially the most common form caused by 21-hydroxylase deficiency. It is used for newborn screening for severe CAH, to help diagnose mild CAH in symptomatic children, teens, and adults, to see whether CAH treatment is working, and to help rule out CAH in women with symptoms such as facial hair and irregular menstrual periods.
associated_symptoms: Rapid growth that stops at a younger age than usual
More facial and/or body hair than usual
Thinning hair on the head, especially near the temples
Endocrine.summary: Normal 17-OHP results suggest CAH with 21-hydroxylase deficiency is unlikely, while higher than normal results suggest CAH. In people being treated for CAH, decreasing 17-OHP levels indicate treatment is working. If results are unclear, an ACTH stimulation test may be ordered for further evaluation.

Endocrine.purpose: Used to help diagnose and monitor conditions that affect cortisol levels, especially disorders of the pituitary and adrenal glands. It is interpreted together with cortisol testing to help identify causes of high or low cortisol.
associated_symptoms: Increased fat around the base of the neck or between the shoulder blades
Wide purple streaks on the stomach, breasts, hips, and under the arms
related_diseases_or_conditions: Tumors outside of the pituitary gland that make extra ACTH
Long-term use of high doses of steroid medicine
Rare type of tumor in the lung, pancreas, or thyroid gland
Endocrine.summary: ACTH is a blood test that measures a pituitary hormone controlling cortisol production by the adrenal glands. Results are usually interpreted alongside cortisol levels: high ACTH with high cortisol suggests ACTH-producing pituitary or ectopic tumors, high ACTH with low cortisol suggests adrenal damage, low ACTH with high cortisol suggests Cushing's syndrome, and low or normal ACTH with low cortisol suggests hypopituitarism.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures aldosterone in blood or urine and is used, often with a renin test, to help determine whether abnormal aldosterone is causing high blood pressure, to diagnose adrenal gland disorders, to evaluate abnormal sodium or potassium levels, and to help find the cause of orthostatic hypotension.
associated_symptoms: high blood pressure that doesn't improve with usual blood pressure medicines
high blood pressure that develops at a young age
dizziness when you get up from sitting or lying down
related_diseases_or_conditions: cancer cells in the adrenal glands
Endocrine.summary: Aldosterone results are interpreted with other tests, especially renin, to determine whether abnormal aldosterone production is due to an adrenal gland problem or another condition affecting the renin-aldosterone system. High levels may suggest primary or secondary aldosteronism, while low levels may suggest adrenal insufficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, or related disorders; results can also be influenced by other conditions and certain medicines.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures C-peptide in blood or urine to estimate how much insulin the pancreas is making naturally; it is used to help evaluate hypoglycemia, monitor and guide diabetes treatment, monitor insulinoma treatment, and sometimes help distinguish between type 1 and type 2 diabetes when the diagnosis is uncertain.
related_diseases_or_conditions: drinking too much alcohol without eating
low level of potassium in the blood
Endocrine.summary: C-peptide reflects the pancreas’s own insulin production because it is released in equal amounts with insulin and lasts longer in the blood. High results usually suggest too much insulin production, while low results suggest insufficient insulin production. In people treated for an insulin-producing pancreatic tumor, falling levels suggest treatment is working and rising levels may suggest the tumor has returned.

Endocrine.purpose: Measure catecholamine levels in urine or blood to help diagnose or rule out certain rare tumors, and to monitor whether treatment for these tumors is working.
associated_symptoms: High blood pressure, especially if it isn't getting better with treatment
Tingling in your arms and legs
An abnormal lump in the abdomen
Weight loss for no known reason
Endocrine.summary: High catecholamine levels in urine or blood can suggest a pheochromocytoma, neuroblastoma, or paraganglioma, but stress, exercise, caffeine, smoking, and alcohol can also raise levels. Results are interpreted along with symptoms, history, and other tests, and high results often lead to additional imaging such as CT or MRI.

Endocrine.purpose: A cortisol test is used to measure cortisol in blood, urine, or saliva to help diagnose or rule out conditions causing too much or too little cortisol, including Cushing's syndrome, Addison disease, and secondary adrenal insufficiency, and to monitor treatment for these conditions.
associated_symptoms: Increased fat around the base of your neck or between your shoulder blades
Wide purple streaks on your stomach, breasts, hips, and under your arms
related_diseases_or_conditions: surgical removal of your pituitary gland
Endocrine.summary: Cortisol results that are too high may suggest Cushing's syndrome or related causes of excess cortisol, while low results may suggest Addison disease or secondary adrenal insufficiency. Because cortisol varies during the day and can be affected by stress, exercise, pregnancy, medicines, and other factors, abnormal results usually need follow-up testing to find the cause.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures DHEA sulfate (DHEAS) in blood to check whether the adrenal glands are working well, help diagnose adrenal gland tumors and disorders of the testicles or ovaries, evaluate early or late puberty in boys, and investigate masculinizing features in women and girls.
associated_symptoms: Excess body and facial hair growth
Hair loss at the top of the head
Endocrine.summary: High DHEAS levels may suggest congenital adrenal hyperplasia, an adrenal gland tumor, PCOS, or rarely an ovarian tumor. Low DHEAS levels may suggest Addison disease or hypopituitarism. Results are interpreted together with symptoms, age, sex, medical history, and other blood tests.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures estrogen levels in blood, urine, or saliva to help diagnose hormone-related conditions, monitor fertility and hormone therapies, and, during pregnancy, assess certain birth defects or high-risk pregnancies.
associated_symptoms: unable to get pregnant after a year of trying
Endocrine.summary: Estrogen test results must be interpreted based on age, sex, pregnancy status, reason for testing, and which estrogen was measured. High or low levels may suggest a health problem; in males, a high level is usually abnormal, while in females levels normally change across puberty, pregnancy, and menopause and may need repeat testing to identify trends.

Endocrine.purpose: Used to determine whether breast cancer cells have estrogen and/or progesterone receptors so hormone receptor status can guide treatment decisions.
Endocrine.summary: ER/PR testing is performed on a breast tissue biopsy to identify whether cancer cells express estrogen and/or progesterone receptors. A positive result means at least 1% of cells have receptors and the cancer may respond to hormone-directed therapy; a negative result means fewer than 1% of cells have receptors and these treatments are unlikely to be effective. Results are used along with other tests, such as HER2 testing, to help plan breast cancer treatment.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures the level of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) in blood to help diagnose causes of infertility, irregular or absent periods, low sperm count, abnormal puberty timing, and disorders of the pituitary gland, hypothalamus, or reproductive glands.
associated_symptoms: early signs of sexual development before age 8 in girls
early signs of sexual development before age 9 in boys
no signs of sexual development by age 13 in girls
no signs of sexual development by age 14 in boys
related_diseases_or_conditions: medical conditions that affect how the ovaries work
medical conditions that affect the testicles
Endocrine.summary: FSH is a pituitary hormone involved in sexual development and reproduction. High levels often suggest the ovaries or testicles are not making normal sex hormones, while low levels may point to pituitary or hypothalamic problems. In children and teens, results help distinguish early puberty, peripheral precocious puberty, or delayed puberty.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures the amount of glucagon in the blood and is used most often to help diagnose hypoglycemia, pancreatitis, and glucagonoma; it may also be used to monitor people with diabetes.
associated_symptoms: Tingling in the lips, tongue, or cheeks
A rash on the face, stomach, or legs
Sores in the mouth or tongue
Endocrine.summary: A glucagon blood test helps evaluate disorders affecting blood glucose regulation. Abnormal results may indicate hypoglycemia, diabetes, pancreatitis, or a glucagon-producing pancreatic tumor; the test is different from a glucagon stimulation test, which assesses growth hormone problems.

Endocrine.purpose: Blood tests used to detect and monitor growth hormone disorders by checking whether the body is making too little or too much growth hormone, and to help evaluate pituitary gland problems.
associated_symptoms: Slowed growth rate compared with children of the same age and sex
Lower weight than children of the same age and sex
Excessive growth compared with children of the same age and sex
Larger than normal hands and feet
Larger than normal facial features such as lips, nose, and tongue
Endocrine.summary: A GH stimulation test that fails to raise GH to the expected level may suggest growth hormone deficiency, while a GH suppression test that fails to lower GH appropriately may suggest growth hormone excess such as gigantism in children or acromegaly in adults. Further testing may be needed to identify the cause, often a pituitary tumor.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures the amount of homocysteine in blood. It is used most often to assess vitamin B6, vitamin B12, and folic acid (folate) levels, help diagnose homocystinuria, and help understand risk for heart attack or stroke in people already at increased risk.
associated_symptoms: changes in the color of your skin or fingernails
sores on your tongue or in your mouth
tingling in your hands, feet, arms, and/or legs
numbness in your hands, feet, arms, and/or legs
Endocrine.summary: Low homocysteine is normal. High levels may suggest inadequate vitamin B6, B12, or folate intake, homocystinuria, or increased risk for cardiovascular and blood vessel disease. Results can also be influenced by age, sex, and smoking, and elevated values do not always mean a condition requiring treatment.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures IGF-1 in the blood to help evaluate growth hormone (GH) levels and detect or monitor growth hormone disorders, including GH deficiency, GH insensitivity (Laron syndrome), gigantism, and acromegaly.
associated_symptoms: Slowed growth rate compared with children of the same age
Lower weight than children of the same age
Excessive growth compared with children of the same age
Larger than normal hands and feet
Larger than normal facial features such as lips, nose, and tongue
Endocrine.summary: IGF-1 is a more stable marker than growth hormone and reflects GH activity over time. Low IGF-1 can suggest GH deficiency or GH insensitivity, while high IGF-1 may indicate gigantism in children or acromegaly in adults, often due to a pituitary tumor. Results are interpreted along with age and other tests, and additional GH or IGFBP-3 testing may be needed.

Endocrine.purpose: Used with other tests to help find the cause of hypoglycemia, diagnose insulin resistance, guide treatment decisions for type 2 diabetes, and monitor how well pancreatic islet cell transplantation surgery is working.
Endocrine.summary: Insulin levels are interpreted together with blood glucose and other test results. High insulin with normal or slightly high glucose may suggest insulin resistance. High or normal insulin with low glucose may indicate too much insulin, such as from insulinoma, Cushing's syndrome, or excess insulin use. Low insulin with high glucose may mean the pancreas is not making enough insulin, as can occur with type 1 diabetes or pancreatitis. A C-peptide test is often done with this test to better estimate how much insulin the pancreas makes.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures the level of luteinizing hormone (LH) in blood or sometimes urine. It is used to help diagnose causes of infertility, irregular or absent periods, ovulation timing, menopause/perimenopause, ovarian or testicular disorders, pituitary or hypothalamic disorders, and early or delayed puberty.
associated_symptoms: unable to get pregnant after 12 months of trying
symptoms that may be related to menopause
unable to get your partner pregnant after 12 months of trying
loss of muscle and/or body hair
Endocrine.summary: LH results are interpreted with age, sex, symptoms, medical history, and other hormone tests, especially FSH. Higher LH can suggest ovulation, menopause transition, ovarian or testicular dysfunction, chromosomal disorders, or damage from autoimmune disease, radiation, or chemotherapy. Lower LH often points to a pituitary or hypothalamic problem, and in children or teens the pattern can help distinguish early, delayed, or peripheral puberty.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures the level of parathyroid hormone in the blood to help evaluate whether the parathyroid glands are regulating calcium properly. It is used to investigate abnormal blood calcium or phosphate levels, monitor chronic kidney disease or known parathyroid disorders, assess severe osteoporosis, check whether treatment is working, and confirm removal of overactive parathyroid tissue during surgery.
associated_symptoms: Bone, joint, and muscle symptoms, such as weakness, aches, and pains
related_diseases_or_conditions: Abnormally low phosphate blood test results
Parathyroid gland damage from neck surgery
Endocrine.summary: PTH results are interpreted together with blood calcium, and sometimes phosphate and other tests, because PTH normally rises and falls in response to calcium levels. High PTH with high calcium suggests primary hyperparathyroidism, high PTH with low calcium suggests secondary hyperparathyroidism, and low PTH with low calcium suggests hypoparathyroidism. Abnormal results may prompt additional blood tests or imaging studies.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures progesterone in blood to help evaluate ovulation and fertility problems, monitor pregnancy and pregnancy complications, assess miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy risk, check response to fertility treatment or progesterone therapy, and help diagnose certain ovarian or adrenal gland disorders and abnormal uterine bleeding.
Endocrine.summary: Progesterone levels vary across the menstrual cycle and pregnancy, so results must be interpreted in context. High values may suggest pregnancy with multiples, molar pregnancy, ovarian cysts, ovarian cancer, or adrenal disorders, while low values may indicate poor ovulation or conditions such as amenorrhea, PCOS, miscarriage risk, ectopic pregnancy, or pre-eclampsia. Repeated testing may be needed because levels change over time.

Endocrine.purpose: A prolactin test is used, usually along with other tests, to help diagnose a prolactinoma, find the cause of irregular menstrual periods, infertility in men and women, and low sex drive and/or erectile dysfunction in men, and to monitor a known prolactinoma to see whether treatment is working or the tumor has returned.
associated_symptoms: Changes in menstruation (irregular periods or absence of periods)
Production of breast milk when not pregnant or breastfeeding
Endocrine.summary: Prolactin levels are normally high in pregnant and breastfeeding women and low in nonpregnant women and men. Higher-than-normal levels may point to a prolactinoma or another underlying condition, while low levels are rare and may suggest a pituitary disorder. The test cannot identify the exact cause by itself, so other tests are often needed.

Endocrine.purpose: A renin test is used, often along with an aldosterone test, to determine whether the adrenal glands are making too much or too little aldosterone and to help diagnose primary aldosteronism (PA).
Endocrine.summary: Renin levels are interpreted with aldosterone levels to help identify adrenal and related disorders. High renin can suggest Addison disease, cirrhosis, or dehydration, while low renin can suggest primary aldosteronism or kidney disease. Specific renin/aldosterone patterns may indicate Cushing's syndrome, PA, Addison disease, or secondary aldosteronism. Results may be affected by medicines, salt intake, body position, stress, and natural black licorice.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) in blood to help estimate how much testosterone is free and active in the body. It is used to help evaluate symptoms of abnormal testosterone levels, support diagnosis or monitoring of hormonal disorders such as PCOS, and help assess early puberty in children.
associated_symptoms: too much hair growth on the face and body
Endocrine.summary: SHBG helps determine how much testosterone is available for tissues to use. Low SHBG usually means more free testosterone, while high SHBG means less testosterone is available. Results are interpreted together with total testosterone to help explain symptoms and identify possible hormonal imbalance.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures thyroid-stimulating hormone in the blood to assess how well the thyroid is working, including detecting hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism and monitoring thyroid hormone treatment.
associated_symptoms: unusual bumps or lumps on your thyroid
Endocrine.summary: A TSH result that is too high or too low can indicate that the thyroid is making too little or too much hormone. The test helps identify thyroid dysfunction, but abnormal results usually need additional thyroid tests to determine the cause; in some cases, abnormalities may reflect a pituitary problem or be influenced by illness, age, or pregnancy.

Endocrine.purpose: Measures testosterone in blood to help find the cause of abnormal testosterone levels, monitor people with previous abnormal results or those taking medicines or hormone therapy that may affect testosterone, and help evaluate early or delayed puberty in children and teens.
associated_symptoms: Difficulty getting or keeping an erection
Lack of face or body hair
Abnormal hair growth on the body or face
Endocrine.summary: A testosterone test alone cannot diagnose a condition, but abnormal results together with symptoms may suggest an underlying health problem. Low or high testosterone can be associated with different disorders depending on sex and age, and testosterone levels normally decrease with age.

Endocrine.purpose: To help determine whether abnormal thyroid hormone test results are caused by an autoimmune thyroid disease, and to check for specific thyroid antibodies associated with Hashimoto's disease or Graves' disease.
Endocrine.summary: A negative result means thyroid antibodies were not found and thyroid symptoms are less likely to be due to an autoimmune disease. A positive result means thyroid antibodies were found, which may indicate Hashimoto's disease or Graves' disease depending on the antibody pattern; higher levels make an autoimmune thyroid disorder more likely.

Endocrine.purpose: Used with other thyroid tests to help diagnose and monitor thyroid disease, including hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, and to gather information about other thyroid, pituitary, or hypothalamic conditions. It may also be used to check a newborn for congenital hypothyroidism and to monitor thyroid hormone treatment.
associated_symptoms: Weight loss, even though you may be eating more than usual
Sweating or being very sensitive to heat
Endocrine.summary: T4 measures thyroid hormone levels in blood, either as free T4 or total T4. Low values may suggest hypothyroidism, Hashimoto's disease, thyroiditis, iodine problems, congenital hypothyroidism, or certain pituitary issues, while high values may suggest hyperthyroidism, Graves' disease, thyroiditis, toxic goiter or toxic nodules, too much iodine, pituitary tumors, or excessive thyroid hormone treatment. Results are interpreted together with TSH and other thyroid tests because many factors, including medicines and severe illness, can affect T4 levels.

Endocrine.purpose: A T3 test measures the level of triiodothyronine in blood to help diagnose thyroid disease, including hyperthyroidism, help identify pituitary disorders, and monitor treatment for thyroid disease.
Endocrine.summary: T3 results are interpreted together with TSH and T4. High T3 may suggest hyperthyroidism, while low T3 may suggest hypothyroidism; normal T3 alone does not rule out thyroid disease. Patterns of TSH and free T4 help distinguish whether the cause is a thyroid gland problem or a pituitary gland condition.

Liver Function.purpose: Measures the amount of ALT in the blood and is used to help screen for, diagnose, and monitor liver damage or disease, usually as part of liver function tests or a comprehensive metabolic panel.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in your abdomen (belly)
Swelling in your ankles and legs
related_diseases_or_conditions: Lack of blood flow to the liver
Certain medicines that can cause liver damage
Liver Function.summary: ALT is an enzyme found mainly in the liver. High blood ALT usually suggests liver cell injury or liver disease, while low levels are uncommon. Results are interpreted with other liver tests and can help distinguish acute from chronic liver problems, but the ALT level does not indicate how much the liver is damaged.

Liver Function.purpose: To help diagnose and monitor liver damage or liver disease, check liver health as part of routine blood screening, and sometimes help diagnose other health conditions.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in your abdomen (belly)
Swelling in your ankles and legs
related_diseases_or_conditions: A family history of liver disease
Taking certain medicines that can cause liver damage
Use of drugs that are toxic to the liver
Liver Function.summary: Low AST levels are usually normal. High AST levels may suggest liver disease or other liver problems, but they can also occur with other conditions or be affected by factors such as pregnancy, exercise, certain medicines, age, and sex. AST is often interpreted together with ALT to assess possible liver damage.

Liver Function.purpose: Measures the amount of albumin in blood to check general health and nutrition, assess how well the liver and kidneys are working, and monitor treatment for liver, kidney, or other conditions that affect albumin levels. It is also often part of liver function tests, a liver panel, or a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP).
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in your abdomen
Swelling in your ankles and legs
Swelling in your hands and feet
related_diseases_or_conditions: Burns over a large area of the body
Liver Function.summary: Low albumin levels may suggest liver disease, kidney disease, malnutrition, infection, digestive problems with protein use, burns, or thyroid disease. High levels may indicate dehydration. Albumin results are not diagnostic by themselves and are interpreted with other tests and clinical findings.

Liver Function.purpose: To screen for, help diagnose, and sometimes monitor diseases of the liver or bones, and to help evaluate other health conditions that can affect alkaline phosphatase levels.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in the abdomen
Swelling in the ankles and legs
Inflammation and arthritis in the joints
Bones that are unusually shaped and/or too large
Liver Function.summary: The alkaline phosphatase test measures ALP in the blood. High ALP can suggest liver or bone disease, but the test alone cannot identify the source, so other tests are often needed. High levels may come from liver problems or bone disorders, while low levels are less common and may indicate nutritional deficiencies, thyroid disease, Wilson disease, or hypophosphatasia.

Liver Function.purpose: To diagnose or rule out alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in people with lung or liver symptoms, to screen people with a family history of the condition, and to help guide treatment for lung disease related to the deficiency.
associated_symptoms: Faster-than-normal heartbeat when you stand up
Asthma that doesn't respond well to treatment
Hardened skin with painful lumps or patches
Liver disease without a known cause
Liver Function.summary: Low alpha-1 antitrypsin blood levels may suggest alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, but a genotype or phenotype test is needed to confirm the diagnosis. The condition can increase risk for lung damage and liver disease, and additional testing may be done to evaluate lung and liver function.

Liver Function.purpose: An ammonia levels test measures the amount of ammonia in blood and is used, along with other tests, to help diagnose the cause of high ammonia levels, monitor conditions that raise ammonia, and check whether treatment is working. It may help evaluate hepatic encephalopathy, Reye syndrome, and urea cycle disorders.
associated_symptoms: Not being sure about the time
Not being sure about where you are
Not being sure who you are
Liver Function.summary: Low ammonia levels are generally normal. High levels usually mean the body is not getting rid of ammonia properly and may be caused by liver disease, kidney disease or failure, urea cycle disorders, Reye syndrome, hepatic encephalopathy, or certain medicines. Elevated results usually require more testing to find the cause and guide treatment.

Liver Function.purpose: To measure bilirubin in the blood and help check liver health, find the cause of jaundice, monitor liver disease or treatment response, and help diagnose newborn jaundice or disorders involving rapid red blood cell breakdown.
Liver Function.summary: Bilirubin levels are interpreted against the lab's reference range. High bilirubin may suggest liver disease or damage, bile duct blockage, or hemolytic anemia, while low levels are usually not concerning but can be associated with certain medicines. Abnormal results can also be influenced by medicines, foods, or strenuous exercise, so results should be discussed with a health care provider.

Liver Function.purpose: Measures bilirubin in urine, usually as part of a urinalysis to help check overall urinary tract health and aid in diagnosing liver problems and other medical conditions.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in the abdomen
Swelling in the ankles and legs
related_diseases_or_conditions: taking certain medicines that can cause liver damage
Liver Function.summary: Bilirubin is normally not found in urine. If it is present, it may be an early sign of liver or bile duct disease. Abnormal results can suggest liver disease such as hepatitis or cirrhosis, or a blockage in the bile ducts, and may lead to more testing such as a liver panel.

Liver Function.purpose: A routine blood test used during checkups to assess overall health, including liver and kidney function, blood glucose, protein levels, fluid and electrolyte balance, and metabolism; it may also help diagnose the cause of symptoms, guide treatment, and monitor whether treatment is working or causing side effects.
Liver Function.summary: A CMP measures 14 blood substances that help evaluate metabolism, liver and kidney health, glucose, proteins, and electrolyte/acid-base balance. Abnormal results can suggest a health condition and usually need follow-up testing and clinical interpretation alongside history and medications.

Liver Function.purpose: Measures the amount of GGT in the blood to help diagnose liver disease, determine whether liver damage is more likely from a liver or bone disorder, check for bile duct blockage, and screen for or monitor alcohol use disorder.
Liver Function.summary: A GGT test reflects possible liver or bile duct injury when blood levels are elevated, but it does not identify the exact cause. It is often interpreted with alkaline phosphatase and other liver tests: high GGT with high ALP suggests liver or bile duct disease, while high ALP with normal or low GGT suggests a bone disorder. Normal or low GGT levels make liver disease less likely.

Liver Function.purpose: To help diagnose and monitor conditions affecting globulin levels, including liver or kidney disease, nutritional problems, autoimmune disorders, immune system disorders, and certain cancers.
associated_symptoms: swelling and/or pain in your abdomen
swelling in your ankles and legs
Liver Function.summary: Globulin tests measure blood proteins made by the liver and immune system. Low globulin levels may suggest liver disease, kidney disease, or malnutrition, while high levels may suggest infection, inflammation, immune disorders, or certain cancers such as multiple myeloma. Abnormal results can also be affected by medicines, dehydration, pregnancy, or other conditions.

Liver Function.purpose: Used as a general test for tissue damage, to help indicate which organs or tissues may be damaged, to help assess how serious the damage may be, and to help diagnose or monitor conditions such as anemia, kidney disease, liver disease, pancreatitis, pulmonary embolism, muscular dystrophy, recent heart attack, and some cancers; it may also be used to see whether treatment is working.
associated_symptoms: symptoms that suggest you have some type of tissue damage
related_diseases_or_conditions: cancer that has spread to different tissues
Liver Function.summary: LDH isoenzyme levels are interpreted in the context of the reason for testing, symptoms, and other test results. High levels of one or more isoenzymes usually suggest tissue damage, and the pattern can help point to the affected organ or condition; for example, LDH-1 higher than LDH-2 may suggest a certain type of anemia, while LDH-5 higher than LDH-4 may suggest liver damage or disease. High results can also occur from intense exercise, some medicines such as aspirin, or specimen hemolysis, while low results are uncommon and usually not considered a health problem.

Liver Function.purpose: Measures LDH in blood or other body fluids to check for tissue damage and help diagnose or monitor a wide range of conditions, including diseases affecting blood, liver, lungs, kidneys, heart, pancreas, brain and spinal cord, as well as some infections and cancers; it can also help monitor treatment response.
Liver Function.summary: LDH is an enzyme found in many tissues; elevated levels usually suggest tissue damage from disease, infection, or injury, but results are not specific and must be interpreted with symptoms and other tests. Low levels are uncommon and usually not a health problem, though they can be seen with high vitamin C or E intake or rare LDH deficiency. If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test may help identify the tissue source of the damage.

Liver Function.purpose: Blood tests used to help find out whether liver disease or damage is causing symptoms, assess how serious diagnosed liver disease is, monitor liver disease and treatment response over time, and check for side effects of medicines that may affect the liver.
associated_symptoms: swelling and/or pain in your abdomen
swelling in your ankles and legs
Liver Function.summary: Liver function tests measure several blood substances made by or associated with the liver. Abnormal results can suggest liver inflammation, hepatitis, impaired liver function, bile duct problems, or liver damage from medicines, but the pattern of results must be interpreted with symptoms, history, and other tests because the panel alone usually cannot diagnose a specific disease.

Liver Function.purpose: Measures prealbumin in the blood. It was used to help assess nutritional status, especially protein intake, and to check for nutrition problems in people at risk of malnutrition, though many clinicians now view it more as a marker of inflammation, infection, or injury than a direct measure of nutrition.
Liver Function.summary: Low prealbumin may be seen with malnutrition, inflammation, trauma, serious illness, liver disease, infection, hyperthyroidism, and certain digestive diseases, while high levels may occur with Hodgkin disease, kidney failure, alcohol use disorder, and high-dose corticosteroid therapy. The test is not considered a definitive measure of nutrition because many other conditions can affect the result.

Liver Function.purpose: Used with other tests to help determine whether autoimmune hepatitis is causing liver damage and to help distinguish type 1 from type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.
associated_symptoms: Abdominal pain in the upper part of your belly
Skin conditions, including rashes, psoriasis, acne, or vitiligo
Liver Function.summary: A positive SMA test means smooth muscle antibodies were found in the blood. High levels often suggest type 1 autoimmune hepatitis, but the test alone cannot diagnose it; biopsy and other tests may be needed. A negative result makes type 1 autoimmune hepatitis less likely, though it does not completely rule out autoimmune hepatitis, especially if other antibodies or clinical findings suggest it.

Liver Function.purpose: A part of urinalysis used to check general health, including the health of the urinary tract and kidneys, and to help diagnose diseases that affect the liver and other medical conditions.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in your abdomen
Swelling in your ankles and legs
Abdominal pain due to an enlarged liver or spleen
related_diseases_or_conditions: Blockage in the ducts that carry bile from your liver or gallbladder to your intestines
Blockage in the blood flow through the liver
Liver Function.summary: Normal urine contains some urobilinogen. High levels may suggest liver disease, hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver damage, or hemolytic anemia, while little or no urobilinogen may suggest bile duct obstruction, impaired bile flow, or other liver problems. The test alone cannot diagnose a specific condition and abnormal results often require follow-up testing.

Tumor Markers.purpose: Measures the level of alpha-fetoprotein in blood to help diagnose, monitor treatment, predict behavior, and check for recurrence of cancers that can produce high AFP, especially liver, ovarian, and testicular cancers; it may also be used to monitor people with chronic hepatitis or cirrhosis for liver cancer risk.
Tumor Markers.summary: AFP is normally very low in healthy children and adults who are not pregnant. High levels can suggest certain cancers, but AFP alone cannot diagnose or rule out cancer because liver injury and noncancer liver diseases can also raise AFP, and some cancers may have normal AFP. Rising AFP during treatment may mean the treatment is not working, decreasing levels may mean it is working, and a later rise after treatment may suggest recurrence.

Tumor Markers.purpose: During pregnancy, the AFP blood test is used to check a baby's risk of certain birth defects and genetic disorders, usually as part of prenatal screening such as a triple screen or quad screen. In people who are not pregnant, it may be used as an AFP tumor marker test to help diagnose certain cancers, especially liver cancer.
Tumor Markers.summary: AFP measures alpha-fetoprotein in blood. In pregnancy, abnormal levels do not diagnose a condition but can indicate increased risk of a fetal problem: low AFP is associated with higher risk of Down syndrome or Edwards syndrome, while high AFP may suggest a neural tube defect, spina bifida, anencephaly, or a defect of the abdomen or esophagus. Results can also be affected by an incorrect due date, multiple pregnancy, or a false positive, so abnormal results usually lead to more testing.

aliases: Quantitative BCR-ABL1 Translocation Detection by RT-PCR
Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL)
Tumor Markers.purpose: Used with other tests to diagnose or rule out chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL). It may also help plan treatment, monitor how well treatment is working, and check for recurrence after treatment.
associated_symptoms: High levels of white blood cells on a complete blood count (CBC) test
Pain or fullness below your ribs on the left side
related_diseases_or_conditions: Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph+ ALL)
Tumor Markers.summary: The test looks for the acquired BCR-ABL1 fusion gene or the Philadelphia chromosome in blood or bone marrow. A positive result, together with abnormal white blood cells and the Philadelphia chromosome, helps confirm certain leukemias. For treatment monitoring, decreasing BCR-ABL1 suggests response to therapy, while increasing levels may mean treatment failure or recurrence.

Tumor Markers.purpose: To measure beta-2 microglobulin levels in blood, urine, or rarely cerebrospinal fluid to help assess the extent of certain blood or bone marrow cancers, predict disease progression, monitor treatment response, and check for spread to the brain or spinal cord when symptoms suggest it. It may also be used to evaluate kidney function, immune/autoimmune disease activity, transplant rejection, and dialysis effectiveness.
Tumor Markers.summary: Higher beta-2 microglobulin levels can be associated with greater cancer burden and, in multiple myeloma, kidney problems. Serial testing can help show whether levels are rising, falling, or stable, which may suggest whether treatment is not working, is working, or whether disease is stable. Because B2M can be elevated in many noncancer conditions, it is not used alone to diagnose cancer.

Tumor Markers.purpose: To measure the CA 19-9 tumor marker in blood, mainly to monitor certain cancers and their treatment, help assess prognosis and cancer stage, check for recurrence after treatment, and sometimes help detect certain cancers when used with other tests.
Tumor Markers.summary: CA 19-9 is a tumor marker that can be elevated in some digestive tract cancers, especially pancreatic cancer, but also in several noncancerous conditions. The test is not used alone to screen for or diagnose cancer; instead, it is interpreted with other tests and, when used for treatment monitoring, changing levels may suggest tumor growth, shrinkage, stability, or recurrence.

Tumor Markers.purpose: Measures the blood level of CA-125, a tumor marker, to help monitor ovarian cancer treatment, check for recurrence, evaluate a suspicious pelvic mass, and in people at very high risk, help screen for ovarian cancer along with other tests.
Tumor Markers.summary: CA-125 is a blood tumor marker that can help monitor ovarian cancer and suggest recurrence or persistent disease when levels rise over time. Falling levels during treatment usually suggest response, but high levels are not specific for ovarian cancer, and normal levels do not rule it out.

Tumor Markers.purpose: A CEA test is used mainly in people already diagnosed with cancers that can raise CEA levels, especially colorectal cancer, to help learn more about the cancer, estimate prognosis or chance of recurrence, monitor how well treatment is working, and check whether cancer has returned.
Tumor Markers.summary: CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen) is a tumor marker that should be very low or absent in healthy adults. It is not used to screen for or diagnose cancer because many cancers may not raise it and noncancer conditions can also increase it. In people with known cancer, lower or decreasing CEA levels may suggest smaller or responding tumors, while rising or persistently high levels may suggest treatment is not working or that cancer has returned, though other tests are needed to confirm the cause.

Tumor Markers.purpose: Used to help diagnose C-cell hyperplasia and medullary thyroid cancer, monitor how well treatment for medullary thyroid cancer is working, check for cancer recurrence after treatment, and screen people at high risk such as those with a family history of MEN 2.
associated_symptoms: A lump in the front of your neck
Swollen lymph nodes in your neck
A change in your voice, such as hoarseness
A long-lasting cough when you don't have a cold
Aches and pains in bones and joints
Tumor Markers.summary: Calcitonin is normally present in small amounts in blood. High levels may suggest medullary thyroid cancer or C-cell hyperplasia, though other conditions can also cause elevation. For people treated for medullary thyroid cancer, falling and staying low levels usually suggest treatment is working, while rising levels may indicate recurrence or spread. Low levels are not known to be a medical problem.

aliases: kappa and lambda free light chains
Tumor Markers.purpose: Measures free light chains in the blood and compares kappa and lambda levels; this ratio can help diagnose and monitor plasma cell disorders and how well treatment is working.
associated_symptoms: Bone pain, often in the back or ribs
Tingling in the arms or legs
Tumor Markers.summary: Abnormal free light chain levels or an abnormal kappa/lambda ratio may suggest a plasma cell disorder such as multiple myeloma, amyloidosis, MGUS, or Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia. Higher levels can also occur with kidney disease, so results are interpreted together with symptoms, medical history, and other blood tests.

Tumor Markers.purpose: To determine whether certain cancers are HER2 positive or HER2 negative by measuring HER2 protein or HER2 gene copies, helping predict how fast the cancer may grow and whether HER2-targeted therapy is likely to work.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Certain other cancers with high HER2 levels
Tumor Markers.summary: HER2 testing is usually done on tumor tissue. Results may be reported by IHC, which scores HER2 protein levels (0/1+ negative, 2+ equivocal, 3+ positive), or by FISH, which reports whether HER2 gene copies are increased. HER2-positive cancers are more likely to respond to HER2-targeted therapy, while HER2-negative cancers generally will not. Tissue testing is preferred; blood tests for HER2 are not generally recommended.

Tumor Markers.purpose: Used to look for gene changes in lung cancer cells, especially non-small cell lung cancer, to help predict how the cancer may behave and guide selection of targeted therapies.
Tumor Markers.summary: This test examines tumor DNA for gene variants or mutations that may affect treatment choices. A positive result may identify a targetable change and support targeted therapy, while a negative result may lead to other treatment options or additional genetic testing. Some results may also show changes that help rule out ineffective therapies or that are not yet understood for treatment decisions.

Tumor Markers.purpose: To measure PD-L1 protein in tumor tissue to help determine whether a patient may benefit from immunotherapy, especially immune checkpoint inhibitors, and to guide treatment choice between immunotherapy alone or in combination with chemotherapy.
related_diseases_or_conditions: head and neck cancer (squamous cell carcinoma)
cancer of the esophagus (squamous cell carcinoma)
Tumor Markers.summary: PD-L1 testing examines tumor tissue for PD-L1 levels. A positive result means the tumor has enough PD-L1 that a specific immunotherapy medicine may help, while a negative result suggests immunotherapy is less likely to be effective and other treatments should be considered. Results may be reported using scoring systems such as CPS or TPS, which vary by test.
