Tumor Markers.purpose: Measures procalcitonin in blood to help determine whether a serious systemic bacterial infection or sepsis is present, distinguish bacterial from viral infections, guide antibiotic treatment decisions, monitor treatment response, and assess sepsis severity; it may also help diagnose kidney infections in children with urinary tract infections.
associated_symptoms: Feeling like you can't get enough air
Tumor Markers.summary: Very high procalcitonin levels suggest sepsis, severe sepsis or septic shock, or a serious systemic bacterial infection. Mild or moderate increases may reflect an early bacterial infection or some noninfectious conditions, while low or decreasing levels can indicate that bacterial treatment is working.

Tumor Markers.purpose: A blood test used to screen for prostate cancer, help diagnose the cause of noncancerous prostate conditions, and monitor treatment for prostate conditions including cancer.
Tumor Markers.summary: The PSA test measures prostate-specific antigen in blood. Low levels are generally normal, while a high PSA can be associated with prostate cancer or several noncancerous conditions such as enlarged prostate, prostatitis, or UTI, and the test cannot determine the exact cause of an abnormal result. Higher PSA results may lead to repeat PSA testing, digital rectal exam, urine testing, or prostate biopsy, and PSA trends can also be used to monitor prostate cancer or response to treatment.

Tumor Markers.purpose: Measures thyroglobulin in blood. It is used mainly to help monitor thyroid cancer after treatment by checking whether thyroid tissue remains, whether treatment was successful, whether cancer may have returned, and how the cancer may behave over time. It may also help evaluate and monitor some noncancerous thyroid conditions such as hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism, and in rare cases thyroid inflammation.
Tumor Markers.summary: Thyroglobulin is a protein made by the thyroid and measured in blood, usually as a tumor marker. After thyroid cancer treatment, very low or absent levels may suggest successful removal of thyroid tissue, while persistent or rising levels may suggest remaining thyroid tissue, recurrent cancer, or spread. Because levels can also change with other thyroid diseases and illnesses, results are usually interpreted over time and in context, and the test may be unreliable if thyroglobulin antibodies are present.

Tumor Markers.purpose: Used mainly after a cancer diagnosis to help determine cancer stage, predict prognosis and chance of recurrence, guide treatment selection, monitor how well treatment is working, and check for remaining or recurrent cancer. Some body-fluid tumor marker tests have a limited role in screening high-risk people or those with symptoms, and tumor cell markers from biopsy tissue may help confirm diagnosis and choose treatment.
associated_symptoms: symptoms that could be from that type of cancer
Tumor Markers.summary: Tumor marker tests measure substances made by cancer cells or by normal cells in response to cancer. Results can help with staging, prognosis, treatment planning, and monitoring, but they are not definitive for diagnosing cancer because levels can be elevated in noncancerous conditions or may be normal even when cancer is present. Biopsy tissue markers may be used with other tests to help confirm a diagnosis.

GI Markers.purpose: Measures the amount of amylase in blood, urine, or sometimes peritoneal fluid. It is mainly used to diagnose and monitor pancreatic disorders, especially pancreatitis, and may also help evaluate salivary gland disorders and certain digestive conditions.
associated_symptoms: Pain in your upper abdomen that may spread to your back
Pain that gets worse after eating
Pain that lasts for several days
related_diseases_or_conditions: A blockage in a duct in the pancreas
Lack of blood flow to the intestines
GI Markers.summary: Amylase results are interpreted by comparing high or low levels with possible pancreatic, salivary gland, digestive, kidney, liver, or pregnancy-related conditions. High blood, urine, or peritoneal fluid amylase can suggest acute pancreatitis or other abdominal problems, while low blood or urine amylase may occur with chronic pancreatic damage or certain systemic diseases.

GI Markers.purpose: To check for inflammation in the intestines and, in most cases, help distinguish inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) from irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). It may also be used to assess IBD severity, guide treatment, monitor whether IBD is improving or worsening, and help predict recurrence.
associated_symptoms: always feeling like you need to move your bowels
pain when you move your bowels
urgent need to move your bowels
related_diseases_or_conditions: food poisoning caused by certain types of bacteria
GI Markers.summary: A calprotectin stool test measures calprotectin, a protein released by white blood cells during intestinal inflammation. Low or normal levels usually suggest the intestines are not inflamed, while high levels suggest inflammation and may prompt further testing such as colonoscopy. Very high levels are often linked to IBD or certain bacterial food poisoning, and somewhat high levels can also occur with cancer, celiac disease, bacterial infection, NSAID use, or treated IBD.

GI Markers.purpose: Used to help diagnose celiac disease, monitor celiac disease, and see whether a gluten-free diet is relieving symptoms. Different antibody tests may be used depending on the situation, including tTG IgA, IgA, IgG, and DGP antibody tests.
associated_symptoms: An itchy rash called dermatitis herpetiformis
GI Markers.summary: A positive result suggests celiac disease, a negative result makes it less likely, and an uncertain result means the diagnosis is unclear. If results are positive or indeterminate, follow-up tests such as biopsy, capsule endoscopy, genetic testing, or tests for related complications may be needed.

GI Markers.purpose: Used to check for pancreatic insufficiency and help diagnose conditions that can cause it, such as pancreatitis and cystic fibrosis, as well as the cause of malnutrition.
GI Markers.summary: This stool test measures chymotrypsin, and sometimes trypsin, to assess how well the pancreas is functioning. Normal levels suggest normal pancreatic enzyme output, while low levels may indicate pancreatic insufficiency, though additional tests are needed to confirm a specific cause.

GI Markers.purpose: A screening test used to check for hidden blood in stool, mainly to help detect colorectal cancer early and to look for other causes of gastrointestinal bleeding or anemia; it may also help distinguish irritable bowel syndrome from inflammatory bowel disease.
GI Markers.summary: A positive FOBT means blood was found in stool, suggesting bleeding somewhere in the digestive tract. It does not diagnose cancer by itself; follow-up testing, often colonoscopy, is usually needed to find the exact cause and location of bleeding.

GI Markers.purpose: A haptoglobin test is used most often to diagnose hemolytic anemia and may also help determine whether another type of anemia or another blood disorder is causing symptoms. It can also help check for a bad reaction to a blood transfusion when used with a direct anti-globulin test.
GI Markers.summary: Haptoglobin is a liver-made protein that binds free hemoglobin in the blood. Low levels can indicate increased red blood cell destruction or other conditions such as liver disease or transfusion reaction, while high levels may be seen with inflammatory conditions, severe infection, diabetes, or some rheumatic and bowel diseases. Results are interpreted together with symptoms, medical history, and other blood tests.

GI Markers.purpose: Used to diagnose lactose intolerance and to check for other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, including irritable bowel syndrome, celiac disease, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis.
GI Markers.summary: Lactose tolerance testing helps determine whether symptoms are due to poor lactose digestion. In a hydrogen breath test, increased breath hydrogen after lactose and worsening symptoms suggests lactose intolerance; in a glucose blood test, little or no rise in blood glucose after lactose suggests lactose intolerance. Normal or negative results make lactose intolerance less likely, though further testing may still be needed in some cases.

GI Markers.purpose: Measures the level of lipase in the blood to help diagnose pancreatic diseases, especially acute pancreatitis, monitor treatment for pancreatic disease, and help diagnose or monitor conditions such as cystic fibrosis, Crohn's disease, celiac disease, intestinal injury or blockage, peritonitis, and pancreatic cysts.
associated_symptoms: Pain in your abdomen that may spread to your lower back
related_diseases_or_conditions: Injury or blockage of the intestines
GI Markers.summary: A high lipase level, especially a very high level, usually suggests acute pancreatitis. Higher-than-normal levels can also be seen with other pancreatic, intestinal, kidney, gallbladder, salivary gland, and metabolic conditions, while low levels may indicate permanent pancreatic damage in chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis or chronic pancreatitis. Some medicines can also affect results.

GI Markers.purpose: A stool elastase test is used to check for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) when a person has belly pain and other digestive symptoms without a known cause. It is also used to monitor pancreatic function in people with cystic fibrosis, diabetes, or chronic pancreatitis, and it is better at detecting severe EPI than mild or moderate disease.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Other surgery on the digestive system
GI Markers.summary: A normal stool elastase level suggests pancreatic exocrine function may be adequate, but it does not completely rule out EPI. A low level may indicate exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, often described as moderate or severe pancreatic insufficiency, and usually prompts additional testing to confirm the diagnosis and determine the cause.

GI Markers.purpose: To determine whether diarrhea is caused by inflammation in the digestive system and to help narrow the cause to conditions that do or do not involve inflammation.
associated_symptoms: Diarrhea for more than a few days
Watery diarrhea three or more times a day that doesn't get better after several days
Diarrhea 6 or more times in 24 hours
GI Markers.summary: A positive result means white blood cells were found in stool, suggesting inflammation in the digestive tract. A negative result means no white blood cells were seen, but it does not fully rule out inflammation because white blood cells break down quickly in stool. The test cannot identify the exact cause of diarrhea and is often used with other tests; fecal calprotectin is a more accurate test for inflammation.

GI Markers.purpose: A xylose test is used to help diagnose malabsorption disorders and to help determine why a child is not gaining weight despite eating enough food.
associated_symptoms: Weight loss for no known reason
Not being able to gain weight
GI Markers.summary: Xylose testing measures blood and urine xylose after drinking a xylose solution to see how well the intestines absorb carbohydrates. High xylose levels are normal, while low blood or urine levels may suggest malabsorption, certain intestinal diseases or infections, and sometimes kidney disease if blood levels are normal but urine levels are low.

Rheumatology.purpose: Used to help diagnose autoimmune disorders, including systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma, Sjögren's syndrome, Addison disease, autoimmune hepatitis, and thyroid diseases.
Rheumatology.summary: An ANA test detects antinuclear antibodies in blood. A negative result makes an autoimmune disorder less likely, though it does not rule one out. A positive result may suggest an autoimmune disease, a short-term viral infection, cancer, or can occur in healthy people, especially older adults and women over 65, so results must be interpreted with other tests and clinical findings.

Rheumatology.purpose: Used to help diagnose autoimmune vasculitis and determine which type is present, monitor treatment for autoimmune vasculitis, and help diagnose inflammatory bowel disease such as ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
associated_symptoms: Changes in vision or loss of vision
Numbness, tingling, and/or weakness in different parts of the body
Shooting pains in the arms and legs
Rheumatology.summary: The ANCA test measures antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies in blood. A negative result suggests ANCAs were not found, while a positive result may support a diagnosis of autoimmune vasculitis and indicate the type of ANCA present; in IBD, ANCA results are interpreted with ASCA and other clinical findings.

Rheumatology.purpose: Used to help diagnose or monitor autoimmune diseases by detecting autoantibodies in blood; different autoantibody tests can help identify organ-specific or systemic autoimmune conditions.
Rheumatology.summary: Autoantibody testing measures antibodies directed against the body's own tissues. A negative result means little or no autoantibodies were found, but it does not rule out autoimmune disease. A positive result shows autoantibodies are present, which does not by itself confirm disease because some healthy people have them. Titer levels and panel patterns (such as ANA or ENA) may help guide diagnosis when interpreted with symptoms, history, and other test results.

Rheumatology.purpose: Used to help diagnose or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, often together with or after a rheumatoid factor (RF) test to improve diagnostic accuracy.
associated_symptoms: Joint stiffness, especially in the morning
Rheumatology.summary: A positive CCP antibody test means these autoantibodies were found in the blood and, especially when combined with a positive RF test and compatible symptoms, strongly suggests rheumatoid arthritis. A negative result makes rheumatoid arthritis less likely, though interpretation depends on RF results, physical exam, and other clinical findings. CCP antibodies can also appear in some other autoimmune disorders and certain infections or chronic lung disease.

Rheumatology.purpose: Measures the levels and/or activity of complement system proteins, either individually (such as C3 and C4) or as total complement activity (CH50/CH100), to help diagnose or monitor autoimmune diseases and sometimes certain infections.
Rheumatology.summary: Low complement levels or activity may suggest the body is attacking its own tissues or clearing foreign substances, and can be seen in autoimmune disease, liver disease, kidney disease, hereditary angioedema, malnutrition, or recurrent infection. High levels may indicate acute or chronic inflammation, certain cancers, or ulcerative colitis, and in someone being treated for an autoimmune disease may mean treatment is working.

Rheumatology.purpose: Used mainly along with other tests to help diagnose rheumatoid arthritis and to check for other autoimmune disorders, certain infections, and certain types of cancer.
associated_symptoms: Joint pain or stiffness when moving
Hard bumps under the skin near the joints
Rheumatology.summary: The RF test measures rheumatoid factor in blood. A positive result suggests a higher level of rheumatoid factor, but the test alone cannot diagnose a disease; results must be interpreted with symptoms, medical history, and other tests. Higher RF levels can be seen in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases, chronic infections, and some cancers, while a normal result does not rule out rheumatoid arthritis.

Rheumatology.purpose: A synovial fluid analysis is used to help diagnose the cause of joint pain and inflammation and to evaluate joint disorders by examining the fluid’s appearance, chemical properties, and microscopic contents for signs of infection, crystals, bleeding, or other disease.
associated_symptoms: A joint that feels warm to the touch
Rheumatology.summary: Synovial fluid is normally light yellow, clear, and slightly sticky or stringy. Abnormal fluid that is cloudy or has changed thickness may suggest arthritis, a bleeding disorder, or bacterial infection. The test results are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, and other test results.

Rheumatology.purpose: Measures uric acid in blood or urine. It is used to help diagnose gout, monitor uric acid levels during cancer chemotherapy or other cancer treatments, evaluate whether uric acid is contributing to kidney stones, and monitor kidney stone risk in people with gout.
associated_symptoms: Sharp pain in your lower abdomen (belly), side, groin or back
Not being able to urinate at all or only urinating a little bit
Rheumatology.summary: Uric acid results help identify or monitor conditions linked to too much or too little uric acid. High blood uric acid may reflect overproduction, reduced kidney removal, diet, gout, kidney disease, some cancers or cancer treatments, alcohol use disorder, or preeclampsia. High urine uric acid may be related to gout, kidney stones, certain cancers, obesity, or inherited disorders; low urine uric acid may occur with kidney disease, lead poisoning, or alcohol use disorder.

Electrolytes.purpose: To assess the acid-base balance of the blood and help determine whether electrolytes are out of balance or whether the blood is too acidic (acidosis) or not acidic enough (alkalosis).
associated_symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the face, hands, or feet
Electrolytes.summary: The anion gap blood test is a calculated value based on electrolyte measurements that helps evaluate blood pH and electrolyte balance. A high anion gap suggests the blood may be too acidic and can be seen with conditions such as acidosis, while a low anion gap may suggest alkalosis and is often associated with low albumin. Abnormal results need to be interpreted with other clinical information and may warrant repeat or additional testing.

Electrolytes.purpose: A BMP is used to screen for, diagnose, or monitor health conditions and to assess kidney function, fluid and electrolyte balance, blood glucose levels, acid-base balance, and metabolism.
associated_symptoms: vomiting that lasts a long time
Electrolytes.summary: A BMP measures eight blood substances that reflect fluid balance, metabolism, kidney function, electrolytes, and blood glucose. Abnormal results, alone or in combination, may indicate an underlying health problem such as kidney disease, breathing problems, or diabetes-related complications, and often require follow-up testing.

Electrolytes.purpose: Measures the amount of calcium in the blood to check general health and to help diagnose or monitor conditions affecting the bones, kidneys, digestive system, thyroid, and parathyroid glands. It may measure total calcium or ionized calcium, with total calcium being the most common and often part of a BMP or CMP.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Cancer that spreads to the bone
Too little calcium in the diet
Electrolytes.summary: A calcium blood test measures calcium in the blood, which is important for nerve, muscle, heart, blood vessel, and hormone function. High or low results can suggest a variety of conditions, but abnormal results do not always mean disease because diet and medicines can affect calcium levels. A normal total calcium result estimates ionized calcium, while an ionized calcium test measures the active free calcium directly.

Electrolytes.purpose: Measures the amount of chloride in the blood. It is used in routine blood screening to check general health and to help diagnose or monitor acid and fluid imbalances and related conditions.
associated_symptoms: Vomiting over a long period of time
Electrolytes.summary: The chloride blood test helps evaluate electrolyte, fluid, and acid-base balance. Abnormal chloride levels may be associated with conditions such as dehydration, kidney disease, heart failure, lung disease, Addison disease, and metabolic acidosis or alkalosis, but abnormal results do not always mean a medical problem and can also be affected by fluid intake, vomiting, diarrhea, or certain medicines.

Electrolytes.purpose: A routine blood test used during checkups to assess overall health, including liver and kidney function, blood glucose, protein levels, fluid and electrolyte balance, and metabolism; it may also help diagnose the cause of symptoms, guide treatment, and monitor whether treatment is working or causing side effects.
Electrolytes.summary: A CMP measures 14 blood substances that help evaluate metabolism, liver and kidney health, glucose, proteins, and electrolyte/acid-base balance. Abnormal results can suggest a health condition and usually need follow-up testing and clinical interpretation alongside history and medications.

Electrolytes.purpose: An electrolyte panel is used to check for electrolyte, fluid, or acid-base (pH) imbalances. It is often part of routine blood screening or a comprehensive metabolic panel, and may also be used to evaluate a possible imbalance of a specific electrolyte.
associated_symptoms: Numbness or tingling in your arms, legs, fingers, and toes
Electrolytes.summary: This blood test measures the main electrolytes, including sodium, chloride, potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, magnesium, and phosphate. Abnormal results can signal problems with fluid balance, acid-base balance, kidney disease, heart disease, diabetes, lung infection, liver disease, malabsorption, or medication effects, and may require follow-up based on which electrolyte is too low or too high.

Electrolytes.purpose: Measures the level of magnesium in the blood to help detect low or high magnesium levels and to help find the cause of abnormal levels of other minerals such as calcium, potassium, and phosphorus.
Electrolytes.summary: A magnesium blood test shows how much magnesium is in the blood, but blood levels may be normal even when body stores are low. Abnormal results can suggest too little or too much magnesium, and interpretation depends on symptoms, medical history, and other test results.

Electrolytes.purpose: Measure the concentration of dissolved particles in blood, urine, or stool to assess fluid balance, kidney function, and possible causes of abnormal water balance, including dehydration, overhydration, poisoning, drug overdose, diabetes insipidus, and chronic diarrhea.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Too much salt in the blood
Too little salt in the blood
Electrolytes.summary: Osmolality tests help evaluate how well the body is maintaining fluid balance by measuring dissolved particles in blood, urine, or stool. Abnormal results may indicate dehydration or overhydration, electrolyte imbalance, poisoning, diabetes insipidus, kidney, liver, or heart disease, stroke, or causes of chronic diarrhea such as laxative abuse or malabsorption.

Electrolytes.purpose: Used with other tests to help diagnose and/or monitor kidney disease, bone disorders, and parathyroid disorders, and to monitor people with poorly controlled diabetes or signs of an acid-base imbalance.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Late stages of chronic kidney disease
Electrolytes.summary: The test measures phosphate (phosphorus) in blood. High phosphate is called hyperphosphatemia and low phosphate is called hypophosphatemia; abnormal results may point to kidney, parathyroid, vitamin D, bone, acid-base, nutrition, or medication-related problems, and are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, calcium, vitamin D, and PTH results.

Electrolytes.purpose: Used, along with other tests, to help determine the cause of high or low phosphate in the blood, find out whether too much phosphate in urine is contributing to kidney stones, and help diagnose kidney problems and parathyroid gland disorders.
associated_symptoms: abnormal blood or urine calcium test
Electrolytes.summary: This 24-hour urine test measures how much phosphate is excreted in urine. Results may be reported as phosphorus or phosphate levels. High urine phosphate can suggest kidney disease affecting phosphate retention or hyperparathyroidism, while low urine phosphate can suggest kidney disease affecting phosphate excretion or hypoparathyroidism. Results can also be influenced by diet, laxatives containing sodium phosphate, and normal growth in children.

Electrolytes.purpose: Measures the amount of potassium in the blood. It is often part of an electrolyte panel and is used to monitor or help diagnose conditions associated with abnormal potassium levels, such as kidney disease, high blood pressure, and heart disease.
Electrolytes.summary: This test measures blood potassium, an important electrolyte needed for normal nerve, muscle, and heart function. High or low results can indicate conditions such as kidney, adrenal, or heart problems, medication effects, fluid loss, or abnormal potassium intake, and very abnormal levels may cause serious health issues.

Electrolytes.purpose: Measures the amount of sodium in the blood. It is used as a routine test to check general health and to help find and monitor conditions that affect fluid balance, electrolytes, and acidity. It is often ordered as part of an electrolyte panel, basic metabolic panel (BMP), or comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP).
related_diseases_or_conditions: Loss of sodium from diarrhea or vomiting
Conditions that cause the body to hold onto extra fluid
Electrolytes.summary: The test measures blood sodium, an important electrolyte for fluid balance, acid-base balance, and normal nerve and muscle function. Results that are too high or too low can suggest dehydration or other medical conditions, but interpretation usually depends on other electrolyte tests and the overall clinical context.

Blood Gas&Acid-Base.purpose: Measures oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, pH, and sometimes bicarbonate in arterial blood to help diagnose lung and breathing problems, kidney disorders, and other conditions affecting acid-base balance, and to monitor whether treatment is working.
associated_symptoms: numbness in hands, feet, or face
recent head or neck injury that could affect breathing
Blood Gas&Acid-Base.summary: An ABG test evaluates how well the lungs bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide, while also assessing blood acidity and bicarbonate balance. Abnormal results can suggest problems with the lungs, kidneys, or metabolism, but the test alone usually cannot provide a diagnosis and often leads to further testing.

Blood Gas&Acid-Base.purpose: Measures the amount of carbon dioxide, mostly in the form of bicarbonate, in the blood. It is often part of an electrolyte panel or metabolic panel and is used to help diagnose or monitor electrolyte imbalances and conditions affecting acid-base balance, including problems involving the kidneys, lungs, liver, or high blood pressure.
Blood Gas&Acid-Base.summary: The test helps assess acid-base (pH) balance and electrolyte status. Abnormal results may indicate that the lungs or kidneys are not removing carbon dioxide properly or that another condition is causing too much or too little CO2 in the blood; medications can also affect results.

Urinalysis.purpose: Measures bilirubin in urine, usually as part of a urinalysis to help check overall urinary tract health and aid in diagnosing liver problems and other medical conditions.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in the abdomen
Swelling in the ankles and legs
related_diseases_or_conditions: taking certain medicines that can cause liver damage
Urinalysis.summary: Bilirubin is normally not found in urine. If it is present, it may be an early sign of liver or bile duct disease. Abnormal results can suggest liver disease such as hepatitis or cirrhosis, or a blockage in the bile ducts, and may lead to more testing such as a liver panel.

Urinalysis.purpose: A urinalysis that includes a test for blood in urine is used to check general health, especially the health of the urinary tract, kidneys, and liver, and to look for other health problems.
Urinalysis.summary: A blood in urine test looks for hematuria, which may be visible as pink, red, or reddish-brown urine or may only be found on urinalysis. Many causes are not serious, such as medicines, intense exercise, sexual activity, or menstruation, but blood in urine can also indicate conditions that need further testing and treatment.

Urinalysis.purpose: Used with other tests to help diagnose kidney stones, evaluate kidney function, assess parathyroid gland problems, investigate the cause of bone disease such as osteoporosis, and help explain abnormal calcium blood test results.
associated_symptoms: Sharp pain in your lower abdomen (belly), back, side, or groin
Muscle cramps and spasms in the face, hands, legs, and feet
related_diseases_or_conditions: Cancer that spreads to the bones
Urinalysis.summary: This 24-hour urine test measures calcium excreted in urine. High or low urine calcium can suggest kidney stones, kidney or parathyroid disorders, bone disease, or other conditions affecting calcium use. Results are also influenced by diet, supplements, and some medicines, so abnormal values do not always mean disease.

Urinalysis.purpose: To look for crystals in a urine sample and determine what they are made of, how large they are, and how many are present. It is used to help diagnose or monitor conditions linked to crystals in urine, including kidney stones, kidney diseases, urinary tract infections, and some metabolic problems.
associated_symptoms: Sharp pains in your lower abdomen (belly), side, groin, or back
Not being able to urinate at all or only urinating a little bit
Urinalysis.summary: A crystals in urine test examines urine under a microscope for crystal type and amount. Small amounts can be normal, but large amounts of certain crystals may suggest an underlying condition, contribute to kidney stones, or reflect factors such as diet, dehydration, or certain medicines.

Urinalysis.purpose: Part of a urinalysis or microscopic urine examination used to count epithelial cells in a urine sample, often during a routine checkup or when urinary tract problems are suspected.
Urinalysis.summary: This test examines urine under a microscope to measure epithelial cells. A small number is usually normal, but a large number or results reported as moderate or many may suggest contamination or a medical condition such as a urinary tract infection, kidney disease, yeast infection, liver disease, or certain cancers. Squamous epithelial cells can also indicate a poorly collected contaminated sample.

Urinalysis.purpose: Used as part of urinalysis to check general health and to help evaluate diabetes when blood testing is difficult, as well as to help assess possible uncommon kidney disorders that cause glucose to spill into the urine.
associated_symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
Urinalysis.summary: Little to no glucose in urine is usually normal, but high urine glucose may suggest diabetes, pregnancy, gestational diabetes, or an uncommon kidney disorder. A urine glucose test alone cannot diagnose a condition, and abnormal results may need follow-up blood tests or other testing.

Urinalysis.purpose: A ketones in urine test is used to measure ketone levels in urine and to help monitor people at risk for high ketone levels, especially to detect ketoacidosis early in people with diabetes or other conditions where the body uses fat for energy instead of glucose.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Exercising too hard for a long time
Urinalysis.summary: Some ketones in urine can be normal, but high ketone levels may indicate that the blood is too acidic and may signal ketoacidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis, which can develop quickly and be life-threatening. Results may be reported as a number or as small, moderate, or large amounts, and should be interpreted with your provider in the context of your diet, activity level, and health conditions.

Urinalysis.purpose: Part of a urinalysis microscopic exam used to check a urine sample for excess mucus during routine health checks, monitoring of medical conditions, or when symptoms suggest a urinary tract infection or another condition causing mucus in the urine.
associated_symptoms: Frequent urge to urinate, even when you have little urine in your bladder
Pain or discomfort in your lower abdomen (belly)
Urinalysis.summary: A normal result usually shows a small or moderate amount of mucus in urine. A large amount of mucus may suggest an underlying condition such as a UTI, STI, kidney stones, IBS, or bladder cancer, and may require additional testing to determine the cause.

Urinalysis.purpose: A urinalysis that includes nitrite testing is used to check general health, including the health of the urinary tract and kidneys, and to help check for a urinary tract infection (UTI).
associated_symptoms: Frequent urges to urinate, even when you have little urine in your bladder
Pain or burning when you pee
Urinalysis.summary: Nitrites in urine may indicate a urinary tract infection because some bacteria convert nitrates to nitrites. However, a negative nitrite result does not rule out infection, since some bacteria do not produce nitrites; other urinalysis findings, especially white blood cells, are also considered.

Urinalysis.purpose: Used, along with other tests, to help determine the cause of high or low phosphate in the blood, find out whether too much phosphate in urine is contributing to kidney stones, and help diagnose kidney problems and parathyroid gland disorders.
associated_symptoms: abnormal blood or urine calcium test
Urinalysis.summary: This 24-hour urine test measures how much phosphate is excreted in urine. Results may be reported as phosphorus or phosphate levels. High urine phosphate can suggest kidney disease affecting phosphate retention or hyperparathyroidism, while low urine phosphate can suggest kidney disease affecting phosphate excretion or hypoparathyroidism. Results can also be influenced by diet, laxatives containing sodium phosphate, and normal growth in children.

Urinalysis.purpose: Measures the amount of protein in urine and is often part of a urinalysis used to check general health, assess the urinary tract, and help diagnose or monitor kidney disease and other health problems. It can help find kidney damage early.
associated_symptoms: Swelling in the hands and feet
Urinalysis.summary: A negative result means there was not too much protein in the urine when tested. A high protein level can be temporary from exercise, dehydration, diet, stress, or pregnancy, but persistent proteinuria is often a sign of kidney disease or kidney damage and may require additional tests to determine the cause.

Urinalysis.purpose: A part of urinalysis used to check general health, including the health of the urinary tract and kidneys, and to help diagnose diseases that affect the liver and other medical conditions.
associated_symptoms: Swelling and/or pain in your abdomen
Swelling in your ankles and legs
Abdominal pain due to an enlarged liver or spleen
related_diseases_or_conditions: Blockage in the ducts that carry bile from your liver or gallbladder to your intestines
Blockage in the blood flow through the liver
Urinalysis.summary: Normal urine contains some urobilinogen. High levels may suggest liver disease, hepatitis, cirrhosis, liver damage, or hemolytic anemia, while little or no urobilinogen may suggest bile duct obstruction, impaired bile flow, or other liver problems. The test alone cannot diagnose a specific condition and abnormal results often require follow-up testing.

Cell Count.purpose: Measures the amount and/or percentage of each type of white blood cell in the blood. It is used as part of routine checkups and to help diagnose, monitor, or determine the cause of infections, immune-related conditions, abnormal white blood cell counts, blood disorders, and some cancers.
Cell Count.summary: This test looks at the different white blood cell types to help evaluate immune function and possible causes of abnormal results. High or low counts can be associated with infection, inflammation, allergies, cancer, bone marrow problems, certain medicines, or other conditions, but abnormal results do not always mean disease.

Cell Count.purpose: A blood smear is used with other tests to help diagnose and monitor a wide variety of blood disorders and other conditions affecting the blood, including blood and bone marrow disorders, certain cancers, infections, and certain parasitic diseases. It helps evaluate the size, shape, number, color, and appearance of blood cells and can also detect parasites.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Cancer that affects the bone marrow
Cancer that affects the lymphatic system
Cell Count.summary: A blood smear does not usually diagnose a condition by itself, but it provides detailed microscopic information about blood cells and can reveal abnormalities such as changes in red cells, white cells, platelets, or the presence of parasites. Abnormal results are interpreted together with symptoms, medical history, and other tests to help identify the underlying cause.

Cell Count.purpose: A CSF analysis measures different substances in cerebrospinal fluid to help diagnose diseases and conditions affecting the brain and spinal cord, including infections, autoimmune disorders, bleeding, tumors, and some neurodegenerative diseases.
associated_symptoms: pain in the arms, legs, body, or face
related_diseases_or_conditions: infection of the brain and spinal cord
cancers that spread to the central nervous system
Cell Count.summary: CSF analysis is a group of tests on cerebrospinal fluid that can show infection, autoimmune disease, bleeding, tumors, or other brain and spinal cord disorders. Abnormal results usually prompt more testing, and suspected bacterial meningitis or another serious infection may require treatment before the final diagnosis.

Cell Count.purpose: A complete blood count is often part of a routine checkup and is also used to monitor conditions or treatments that may affect blood cell counts, including infections, anemia, immune system disorders, and blood cancers. It can help diagnose blood diseases, infections, immune system disorders, or other medical conditions and check for changes in an existing blood disorder.
Cell Count.summary: A CBC measures the number and size of major blood cell types and related values, including red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, hemoglobin, hematocrit, and MCV. Abnormal results can suggest conditions such as dehydration, anemia, heart disease, iron deficiency, infection, autoimmune or bone marrow disorders, cancer, or a reaction to medicine, but abnormal values do not always mean a disease is present.

Cell Count.purpose: Measures the percentage of blood made up of red blood cells. It is often part of a complete blood count (CBC) and is used to check general health and to monitor or help diagnose blood disorders such as anemia and polycythemia (erythrocytosis).
associated_symptoms: Shortness of breath when lying down
Skin symptoms such as itching after a shower or bath
Blurred or double vision and blind spots
related_diseases_or_conditions: Cancers that spread to the bone marrow
Cell Count.summary: A hematocrit test reports the percentage of blood made up of red blood cells. Low results may suggest blood loss, anemia, bone marrow problems, or certain cancers, while high results may suggest too many red blood cells or dehydration. Results can also be affected by pregnancy and living at high altitudes.

Cell Count.purpose: Measures the amount of hemoglobin in the blood, usually as part of a complete blood count (CBC), to check for anemia and help evaluate or monitor conditions that can affect hemoglobin levels.
Cell Count.summary: A hemoglobin test shows how much hemoglobin is in your blood and helps assess red blood cell health. Abnormal results can suggest anemia or other conditions, but the test does not identify the exact cause. Low levels may indicate conditions such as anemia, iron deficiency, blood loss, or nutrient deficiencies, while high levels may be seen with lung or heart disease, polycythemia vera, sleep apnea, or sometimes high altitude.

Cell Count.purpose: Measures the average size of red blood cells. It is often part of a complete blood count to check general health and, along with other tests, to help diagnose or monitor blood disorders such as anemia and determine the type of anemia.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Chronic (long-lasting) conditions that could lead to anemia
Conditions affecting the body's ability to use vitamin B12, including certain autoimmune diseases
Cell Count.summary: MCV reflects average red blood cell size. Small cells can suggest iron deficiency anemia or thalassemia, while large cells can suggest vitamin B12/folate-related problems, liver disease, or pernicious anemia. A normal MCV does not rule out anemia, and results must be interpreted with other tests and medical history.

Cell Count.purpose: To measure the average size of platelets, helping diagnose or monitor blood-related conditions and other health conditions, often along with a platelet count and as part of a CBC.
associated_symptoms: Bleeding that takes a long time to stop, even from minor cuts
Small red or purplish spots on the skin
Pain and burning in the feet and hands
Cell Count.summary: MPV measures the average size of your platelets. High MPV suggests larger, younger platelets and may be seen when platelets are being destroyed faster or when the bone marrow is making more new platelets. Low MPV suggests smaller platelets and may indicate reduced production of new platelets. MPV cannot diagnose a condition by itself and should be interpreted with platelet count and other test results.

Cell Count.purpose: Used to measure the number of platelets in the blood and/or assess how well platelets function to help diagnose or monitor problems with bleeding or clotting, evaluate platelet disorders, check bleeding risk before or during surgery, and monitor the effects of blood-thinning medicines.
associated_symptoms: Bleeding for a long time after a minor cut or injury
Pinpoint sized red spots on the skin
Purplish, red, or brown spots on your skin
Menstrual periods that last a long time
Pain, swelling, and warmth in your lower legs
related_diseases_or_conditions: Infection or damage to the bone marrow
Cell Count.summary: Platelet tests help determine whether platelet number or function is abnormal. Low platelet counts can cause excessive bleeding, while high counts can increase clotting risk; abnormal function tests may suggest inherited or acquired platelet disorders, and results are interpreted along with symptoms, history, and other blood tests.

Cell Count.purpose: The RDW blood test is usually part of a complete blood count (CBC) and is used to help diagnose anemia and determine its cause. It may also be used with other tests to help diagnose other conditions, including thalassemia.
Cell Count.summary: RDW measures how much red blood cell size and volume vary. A high RDW means the cells vary more than normal and may suggest an underlying medical condition, while a normal or low RDW does not rule out anemia or other disorders. Results are interpreted with other blood tests to help evaluate conditions such as iron deficiency, different anemias, thalassemia, and sickle cell anemia.

Cell Count.purpose: A red blood cell (RBC) count measures the number of red blood cells in the blood and is usually part of a complete blood count (CBC). It is used to help diagnose red blood cell disorders, such as anemia, and to check for counts that are too low or too high.
Cell Count.summary: The RBC count shows whether red blood cell levels are normal, low, or high. Abnormal results can be an early sign of illness and may prompt further testing such as reticulocyte count, iron tests, or vitamin B tests to help identify the cause.

Cell Count.purpose: Part of a complete blood count used to measure red blood cell size, shape, and hemoglobin characteristics in order to help diagnose different types of anemia.
Cell Count.summary: RBC indices include MCV, MCH, MCHC, and RDW. Abnormal results can suggest different types of anemia and help distinguish among causes based on whether red blood cells are smaller or larger than normal, or whether hemoglobin amount/concentration or size variation is abnormal. RDW alone is not enough for diagnosis and is interpreted with other blood tests and clinical information.

Cell Count.purpose: Measures the number of reticulocytes (immature red blood cells) in the blood to help assess bone marrow production, diagnose and monitor certain types of anemia, and check marrow function after chemotherapy or bone marrow transplant.
Cell Count.summary: A reticulocyte count shows how well the bone marrow is making new red blood cells. High results can suggest hemolysis or bleeding, while low results can suggest impaired production such as iron deficiency, pernicious anemia, aplastic anemia, kidney disease, cirrhosis, or bone marrow failure. Results are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, and other blood tests.

Cell Count.purpose: To measure the total number of white blood cells in the blood and help diagnose or monitor conditions associated with high or low white blood cell counts.
associated_symptoms: Wound that is red, has pus, or won't heal
related_diseases_or_conditions: Tissue damage from a burn injury
Cancer that affects the bone marrow
Cell Count.summary: A WBC test measures how many white blood cells are in the blood. High counts (leukocytosis) may occur with infection, inflammation, allergy, certain cancers, tissue injury, smoking, stress, pregnancy, or some medicines; low counts (leukopenia) may reflect bone marrow damage, immune disorders such as HIV or lupus, cancers affecting the marrow, liver or spleen disease, or chemotherapy. Results are usually interpreted with other blood tests, such as a blood differential.

Metabolic.purpose: To measure glucose in the blood and help screen for, diagnose, and monitor prediabetes, diabetes, gestational diabetes, other causes of abnormal blood glucose, and medication effects on glucose levels.
associated_symptoms: sores that are slow to heal
numbness or tingling in your feet or hands
having trouble seeing or speaking clearly
Metabolic.summary: Blood glucose testing measures the amount of glucose in the blood. Higher-than-normal results may suggest prediabetes or diabetes, though other endocrine, pancreatic, stress-related, liver, kidney, and medication-related causes are possible. Low results may reflect diabetes treatment effects or other medical conditions. The meaning depends on the specific test used, other test results, and medical history.

Metabolic.purpose: To measure cholesterol and triglyceride levels in the blood, estimate risk for heart disease and related cardiovascular problems, and help guide steps to lower high cholesterol.
Metabolic.summary: This blood test measures total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides. Low LDL and high HDL are generally better for heart health, while high LDL and triglycerides can increase the risk of plaque buildup in arteries and future cardiovascular disease. Results may be calculated or directly measured, and healthy targets depend on age and other risk factors.

Metabolic.purpose: A routine blood test used during checkups to assess overall health, including liver and kidney function, blood glucose, protein levels, fluid and electrolyte balance, and metabolism; it may also help diagnose the cause of symptoms, guide treatment, and monitor whether treatment is working or causing side effects.
Metabolic.summary: A CMP measures 14 blood substances that help evaluate metabolism, liver and kidney health, glucose, proteins, and electrolyte/acid-base balance. Abnormal results can suggest a health condition and usually need follow-up testing and clinical interpretation alongside history and medications.

Metabolic.purpose: Diabetes tests are used to screen for, monitor, and diagnose diabetes, prediabetes, and gestational diabetes by measuring blood glucose, and sometimes urine glucose, levels.
associated_symptoms: Sores that are slow to heal
Numbness or tingling in your feet
Metabolic.summary: Results can indicate a healthy glucose level, prediabetes, type 1 or type 2 diabetes, or gestational diabetes. Blood tests are the main way to diagnose and monitor diabetes, with urine tests used less often because they are less accurate. Hemoglobin A1c reflects average glucose over the past three months, and abnormal results may require follow-up testing or ongoing monitoring.

Metabolic.purpose: Used as part of urinalysis to check general health and to help evaluate diabetes when blood testing is difficult, as well as to help assess possible uncommon kidney disorders that cause glucose to spill into the urine.
associated_symptoms: Numbness or tingling in the hands or feet
Metabolic.summary: Little to no glucose in urine is usually normal, but high urine glucose may suggest diabetes, pregnancy, gestational diabetes, or an uncommon kidney disorder. A urine glucose test alone cannot diagnose a condition, and abnormal results may need follow-up blood tests or other testing.

Metabolic.purpose: Measures average blood glucose over the past 2 to 3 months and is used to screen for or diagnose type 2 diabetes and prediabetes, as well as to monitor diabetes or prediabetes control.
associated_symptoms: Numb or tingling hands or feet
Metabolic.summary: The A1C test reflects the percentage of hemoglobin coated with glucose and provides an estimate of average blood sugar over the previous 2 to 3 months. Higher-than-normal results suggest diabetes or prediabetes, while normal results are below 5.7%, prediabetes is 5.7% to 6.4%, and diabetes is 6.5% or higher. Results can be affected by pregnancy, certain medicines, and conditions that alter red blood cells, kidney function, or liver function.

Metabolic.purpose: To measure ketone levels in blood, mainly to check for diabetic ketoacidosis in people with diabetes, and to help assess ketoacidosis risk in people with symptoms or conditions that cause the body to burn fat for energy instead of glucose.
associated_symptoms: Urinating (peeing) a lot more than usual
Breath that has a fruity smell
Metabolic.summary: A normal or negative result usually means ketone production is not excessive and ketoacidosis is unlikely, though early diabetic ketoacidosis may not always be ruled out. A high or positive result means ketones are present; very high levels with symptoms may indicate ketoacidosis, a serious condition that requires prompt treatment and may require hospitalization.

Metabolic.purpose: A ketones in urine test is used to measure ketone levels in urine and to help monitor people at risk for high ketone levels, especially to detect ketoacidosis early in people with diabetes or other conditions where the body uses fat for energy instead of glucose.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Exercising too hard for a long time
Metabolic.summary: Some ketones in urine can be normal, but high ketone levels may indicate that the blood is too acidic and may signal ketoacidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis, which can develop quickly and be life-threatening. Results may be reported as a number or as small, moderate, or large amounts, and should be interpreted with your provider in the context of your diet, activity level, and health conditions.

Metabolic.purpose: Measures lactate (lactic acid) in blood, and sometimes cerebrospinal fluid, to help diagnose and monitor lactic acidosis and other conditions that raise lactate; it may also help evaluate meningitis and distinguish bacterial from viral infection when CSF is tested.
Metabolic.summary: A lactate test shows whether lactate is abnormally high, but it cannot identify the cause by itself. Mild to moderate elevation is called hyperlactatemia, while higher persistent elevation with acidic blood indicates lactic acidosis, which is more serious and needs prompt treatment. When cerebrospinal fluid is tested, high lactate suggests bacterial meningitis, while normal or slightly high lactate suggests viral meningitis.

Metabolic.purpose: Measures methylmalonic acid in blood or urine and is most often used to help diagnose vitamin B12 deficiency; it is also used in newborn screening to check for methylmalonic acidemia.
Metabolic.summary: Higher-than-normal MMA levels may indicate vitamin B12 deficiency, though the test cannot determine the degree of deficiency and may be interpreted with other tests such as homocysteine and vitamin B tests. In babies, moderate or high MMA can suggest methylmalonic acidemia, a rare genetic disorder that can cause life-threatening complications if untreated.

Metabolic.purpose: Used to measure porphyrin levels in blood, urine, or stool to help diagnose or monitor porphyria, including acute and cutaneous forms.
associated_symptoms: pain in the arms and legs
skin blisters when skin is in sunlight
fragile skin that is easily wounded
Metabolic.summary: Small amounts of porphyrins are normal, but high levels in blood, urine, or stool may suggest porphyria. Abnormal results usually lead to additional testing to confirm the diagnosis and determine the type of porphyria. The condition has no cure, but it can often be managed.

Metabolic.purpose: Used to measure triglyceride levels in blood to assess risk for heart disease, stroke, and other artery-related conditions, and to monitor heart conditions and treatment aimed at lowering cardiovascular risk.
Metabolic.summary: The test measures triglycerides, a blood fat. High levels usually do not cause symptoms but can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, artery disease, and, when very high, pancreatitis. Borderline or high results may lead to lifestyle changes, medicine, or further testing such as apo B.

Renal Function.purpose: Measures the amount of urea nitrogen in the blood and is used as part of a comprehensive metabolic panel to help diagnose or monitor kidney disease and to check kidney function.
associated_symptoms: Needing to go to the bathroom (urinate) frequently
Needing to go to the bathroom (urinate) infrequently
Swelling in the arms, legs, or feet
related_diseases_or_conditions: Smoking or using other tobacco products
Renal Function.summary: A BUN test measures urea nitrogen, a waste product normally removed by the kidneys. High BUN levels can suggest the kidneys are not working well, but results can also be affected by age, sex, dehydration, diet, medicines, and other conditions. Low levels may occur with poor protein intake, malnutrition, or liver disease.

Renal Function.purpose: A urinalysis that includes a test for blood in urine is used to check general health, especially the health of the urinary tract, kidneys, and liver, and to look for other health problems.
Renal Function.summary: A blood in urine test looks for hematuria, which may be visible as pink, red, or reddish-brown urine or may only be found on urinalysis. Many causes are not serious, such as medicines, intense exercise, sexual activity, or menstruation, but blood in urine can also indicate conditions that need further testing and treatment.

Renal Function.purpose: A routine blood test used during checkups to assess overall health, including liver and kidney function, blood glucose, protein levels, fluid and electrolyte balance, and metabolism; it may also help diagnose the cause of symptoms, guide treatment, and monitor whether treatment is working or causing side effects.
Renal Function.summary: A CMP measures 14 blood substances that help evaluate metabolism, liver and kidney health, glucose, proteins, and electrolyte/acid-base balance. Abnormal results can suggest a health condition and usually need follow-up testing and clinical interpretation alongside history and medications.

Renal Function.purpose: Measures creatinine in blood and/or urine to help check kidney health, diagnose kidney disease, monitor known kidney problems and treatment response, and assess possible kidney side effects from medicines. Results are often used with eGFR, creatinine clearance, UACR, BUN, or as part of a CMP or BMP to better evaluate kidney function.
associated_symptoms: Swelling in the hands and feet
related_diseases_or_conditions: Poor blood flow to the kidneys
Renal Function.summary: Creatinine is a normal waste product removed by the kidneys. High blood or urine creatinine can suggest kidney dysfunction, but normal results do not always exclude early kidney disease. Abnormal results are often interpreted with eGFR, creatinine clearance, UACR, BUN, and other kidney tests to better assess kidney health.

Renal Function.purpose: Used to screen for kidney disease in people without symptoms, help diagnose and assess how serious kidney disease is, monitor chronic kidney disease and the effects of potentially kidney-harming medicines, and check kidney health before certain treatments.
Renal Function.summary: The GFR test estimates how well the kidneys filter blood each minute, usually by using creatinine and sometimes cystatin C. A normal eGFR generally suggests no kidney disease, while a low or very low eGFR may indicate kidney disease or kidney failure. Results should be interpreted with clinical context because eGFR is not a perfect test and can be abnormal even without kidney damage.

Renal Function.purpose: Used to look for early signs of kidney disease, especially in people at high risk without symptoms, and to monitor kidney disease or treatment effectiveness.
related_diseases_or_conditions: family history of high blood pressure
Renal Function.summary: The test measures albumin in urine compared with creatinine. Abnormal or rising albumin can indicate kidney damage or early kidney disease, but temporary increases can also occur from exercise, fever, inflammation, certain medicines, or other conditions. Abnormal results are often confirmed with repeat testing and may lead to additional kidney tests such as eGFR.

Renal Function.purpose: Used with other tests to help diagnose and/or monitor kidney disease, bone disorders, and parathyroid disorders, and to monitor people with poorly controlled diabetes or signs of an acid-base imbalance.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Late stages of chronic kidney disease
Renal Function.summary: The test measures phosphate (phosphorus) in blood. High phosphate is called hyperphosphatemia and low phosphate is called hypophosphatemia; abnormal results may point to kidney, parathyroid, vitamin D, bone, acid-base, nutrition, or medication-related problems, and are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, calcium, vitamin D, and PTH results.

Renal Function.purpose: Used, along with other tests, to help determine the cause of high or low phosphate in the blood, find out whether too much phosphate in urine is contributing to kidney stones, and help diagnose kidney problems and parathyroid gland disorders.
associated_symptoms: abnormal blood or urine calcium test
Renal Function.summary: This 24-hour urine test measures how much phosphate is excreted in urine. Results may be reported as phosphorus or phosphate levels. High urine phosphate can suggest kidney disease affecting phosphate retention or hyperparathyroidism, while low urine phosphate can suggest kidney disease affecting phosphate excretion or hypoparathyroidism. Results can also be influenced by diet, laxatives containing sodium phosphate, and normal growth in children.

Renal Function.purpose: Measures the amount of protein in urine and is often part of a urinalysis used to check general health, assess the urinary tract, and help diagnose or monitor kidney disease and other health problems. It can help find kidney damage early.
associated_symptoms: Swelling in the hands and feet
Renal Function.summary: A negative result means there was not too much protein in the urine when tested. A high protein level can be temporary from exercise, dehydration, diet, stress, or pregnancy, but persistent proteinuria is often a sign of kidney disease or kidney damage and may require additional tests to determine the cause.

Renal Function.purpose: Measures uric acid in blood or urine. It is used to help diagnose gout, monitor uric acid levels during cancer chemotherapy or other cancer treatments, evaluate whether uric acid is contributing to kidney stones, and monitor kidney stone risk in people with gout.
associated_symptoms: Sharp pain in your lower abdomen (belly), side, groin or back
Not being able to urinate at all or only urinating a little bit
Renal Function.summary: Uric acid results help identify or monitor conditions linked to too much or too little uric acid. High blood uric acid may reflect overproduction, reduced kidney removal, diet, gout, kidney disease, some cancers or cancer treatments, alcohol use disorder, or preeclampsia. High urine uric acid may be related to gout, kidney stones, certain cancers, obesity, or inherited disorders; low urine uric acid may occur with kidney disease, lead poisoning, or alcohol use disorder.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To detect changes in the BRAF gene in cancer so results can help diagnose certain cancers, guide treatment choices, predict how fast a cancer may grow, and determine whether targeted therapy is likely to help. It may also be used to check for inherited BRAF gene changes in people with a personal or family history suggesting increased cancer risk or a BRAF-related genetic condition.
related_diseases_or_conditions: genetic conditions caused by BRAF gene changes
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A BRAF genetic test looks for BRAF gene changes in tumor tissue, blood, or bone marrow. In cancer, a positive result may support targeted treatment; a negative result means another treatment is usually chosen. If an inherited BRAF change is found, it may increase cancer risk or indicate a BRAF-related genetic condition, but it does not mean cancer will definitely occur.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To look for harmful changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes that increase the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancers.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A BRCA genetic test detects whether you have a harmful, uncertain, or negative BRCA1/BRCA2 variant. A positive result means a cancer-risk–increasing variant is present, but it does not predict whether you will develop cancer; results must be interpreted with your personal and family history.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: A blood test used with other tests to help diagnose Wilson disease and other conditions involving too much or too little copper, and to monitor abnormal copper levels and treatment response.
associated_symptoms: Urine that's a darker color than usual
A type of anemia, called hemolytic anemia
Swelling from fluid buildup in your belly, lower legs, or feet
Sudden jerky movements you can't control
Green, gold, or brown rings around your irises
Abnormally low levels of white blood cells called neutrophils
Tingling in your hands and feet
Hair that is colorless, thin, breaks easily, and becomes unusually tangled
related_diseases_or_conditions: Too much copper in the blood
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: Ceruloplasmin is a copper-carrying protein made by the liver. Low levels may suggest problems using or obtaining copper, including Wilson disease, Menkes syndrome, severe liver disease, kidney disease, or copper deficiency, while high levels may be associated with inflammatory or other conditions. Results must be interpreted along with copper tests and the patient’s symptoms and history.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: Cord blood testing is used after birth to assess a newborn’s health by measuring things such as blood gases, bilirubin, blood culture results, complete blood count, glucose, and possible drug exposure. Cord blood banking saves the stem cells in cord blood for possible future treatment of certain blood disorders, cancers, and some inherited metabolic and immune system disorders.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: Cord blood testing can help evaluate a newborn’s oxygen/acid-base status, bilirubin, blood count, glucose, infection, and drug exposure. Cord blood banking preserves stem cells that may later be used in transplants to treat certain diseases; public donation is free, while private banking is usually paid and is mainly recommended when there is a specific family or personal medical need.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To screen for or diagnose Down syndrome during pregnancy, after birth if a baby shows physical signs, or during IVF; screening tests estimate the chance of Down syndrome, while diagnostic tests confirm whether it is present by examining fetal or newborn cells, chromosomes, or DNA.
associated_symptoms: physical signs of Down syndrome after birth
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: Down syndrome tests include prenatal screening and diagnostic tests. Screening tests estimate the risk that a fetus has Down syndrome, while diagnostic tests such as amniocentesis, CVS, PUBS, or karyotype testing can confirm the diagnosis by evaluating fetal or newborn chromosomes or DNA. A positive screening result means increased risk, not a definite diagnosis; a negative result lowers the likelihood but does not rule it out.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: Used to find out if a child has a fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD); early diagnosis and treatment may help reduce symptoms and support development.
associated_symptoms: smooth skin surface between the nose and upper lip
lower than average height and weight
related_diseases_or_conditions: Neurobehavioral Disorder Associated with Prenatal Alcohol Exposure (ND-PAE)
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: This is not a single laboratory test; it is a clinical screening based on physical exam, growth, developmental, and behavioral findings, sometimes using the 4-digit code. A positive screening suggests an FASD and may lead to diagnosis and supportive treatment, while there are no special preparations or risks for the screening.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To check whether a person has an inherited glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: Lower than normal G6PD levels indicate G6PD deficiency. In women, slightly low levels may indicate carrier status. Normal G6PD levels in men make deficiency unlikely, though the test may need to be repeated after a hemolytic episode. People with G6PD deficiency can often prevent symptoms by avoiding trigger substances.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To help diagnose galactosemia in a baby and identify whether it is due to GALT, GALK, or GALE deficiency.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: This newborn blood screening test checks for galactosemia, a rare inherited metabolic disorder that prevents a baby from breaking down galactose. A positive result usually requires confirmatory testing, while early diagnosis and dietary treatment can help prevent serious complications.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To examine the size, shape, and number of chromosomes in cells to detect chromosome abnormalities, help evaluate family members or a fetus for chromosome problems, investigate infertility, recurrent miscarriages, or stillbirths, and assist in diagnosing and guiding treatment for certain cancers and blood disorders.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A normal result means 46 chromosomes with no unusual structural changes. An abnormal result means there are changes in chromosome number or structure, which may indicate a genetic condition, explain reproductive problems, or help diagnose and guide treatment for cancer or blood disorders.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: Looks for the two most common MTHFR gene variants, C677T and A1298C, usually when homocysteine levels are high, to help determine whether the variants may be contributing to elevated homocysteine and to estimate possible risk for blood clots or early heart/blood vessel disease in selected cases. It may also be used to help guide methotrexate dosing or follow up a positive newborn homocystinuria screen.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: The test identifies whether one or both of the common MTHFR variants are present. A positive result may or may not explain elevated homocysteine, and having one variant alone is unlikely to cause health problems. If homocysteine is high, C677T/C677T or C677T/A1298C is more likely to be contributing than A1298C/A1298C. A negative result means the common variants were not found, so another cause of elevated homocysteine should be considered.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: Used to look for changes in the PTEN gene. It may help determine whether PTEN changes are involved in cancer and may guide treatment choices, or detect inherited PTEN changes in people with symptoms of PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome (PHTS) or a family history of PTEN gene changes.
associated_symptoms: many hamartomas, especially in the mouth and intestines, or on the breasts or skin
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: The test looks for acquired or inherited PTEN gene changes. Acquired changes may be found in cancer and can affect treatment and disease behavior. Inherited PTEN changes can indicate PHTS, which does not mean cancer is present but does mean cancer risk is higher and preventive screening and management may be needed.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To screen newborns for high blood levels of phenylalanine (Phe), which may indicate phenylketonuria (PKU) and allow early treatment to prevent brain damage and other serious health problems.
associated_symptoms: A musty odor in the breath, skin, and/or urine (pee)
Psychiatric problems such as mental health disorders
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A normal result means phenylalanine is in the expected range and PKU is unlikely, though very early testing may need to be repeated. A high result suggests PKU and usually requires follow-up testing to confirm the diagnosis; if PKU is present, early dietary treatment is important to prevent permanent nervous system and brain damage.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: To detect human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in urine or blood to determine whether a person is pregnant; quantitative blood tests may also help estimate fetal age early in pregnancy, monitor high-risk pregnancies, and evaluate conditions such as ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, or fetal/chromosomal problems.
associated_symptoms: feeling bloated or swollen in your abdomen
cramping on one side of the pelvis
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A pregnancy test measures hCG in urine or blood. A positive result usually means pregnancy, while a negative result may be false if the test is done too early. Quantitative blood hCG levels can also provide information about pregnancy progression and help evaluate certain pregnancy complications or other hCG-producing conditions.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: A blood screening test used during pregnancy to assess whether an unborn baby is at increased risk for certain chromosome disorders, especially Down syndrome (trisomy 21), Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18), and Patau syndrome (trisomy 13). It may also be used to help determine fetal sex and check Rh blood type.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: Prenatal cfDNA screening analyzes fetal DNA circulating in the mother's blood. It is a low-risk screening test, not a diagnostic test, so a positive result means increased risk rather than a confirmed diagnosis. Negative results make the listed chromosome disorders less likely, but abnormal results usually need confirmation with tests such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling (CVS).

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: A group of blood tests done early in pregnancy to screen for diseases and infections that could affect the pregnant person and developing baby, guide treatment, and help prevent complications.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: The prenatal panel is an early pregnancy blood screening panel that checks blood count, blood type/Rh status, immunity to rubella, and infections such as hepatitis B/C, STIs, and HIV. Abnormal results may lead to treatment during pregnancy or shortly after birth, such as Rh-prevention medicine, infection treatment, hepatitis B vaccination for the baby, or rubella vaccination after delivery.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: Measures sex hormone binding globulin (SHBG) in blood to help estimate how much testosterone is free and active in the body. It is used to help evaluate symptoms of abnormal testosterone levels, support diagnosis or monitoring of hormonal disorders such as PCOS, and help assess early puberty in children.
associated_symptoms: too much hair growth on the face and body
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: SHBG helps determine how much testosterone is available for tissues to use. Low SHBG usually means more free testosterone, while high SHBG means less testosterone is available. Results are interpreted together with total testosterone to help explain symptoms and identify possible hormonal imbalance.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: Measures the quantity and quality of semen and sperm. It is used to help find problems causing infertility and to check whether a vasectomy was successful by confirming whether sperm are present in the semen.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A semen analysis evaluates semen volume, sperm count, concentration, motility, morphology, pH, liquefaction time, and sometimes white blood cells. Abnormal results may suggest a fertility problem, but they do not mean permanent infertility. The test can also confirm whether sperm are absent after a vasectomy.

Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.purpose: The test looks for changes in the TP53 gene. It may be used to help choose treatment for people with cancer and to check for inherited TP53 changes in people with a personal or family history suggesting Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
Genetic/Reproductive/Pregnancy.summary: A TP53 genetic test can identify acquired or inherited TP53 gene changes. In people with cancer, an acquired TP53 change may help guide treatment and predict how the cancer may behave. An inherited TP53 change in one copy of the gene indicates Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which raises the risk of certain cancers, but does not mean a person currently has cancer.

Infection Markers.purpose: Measures the level of c-reactive protein in blood to assess how much inflammation is present in the body, help look for acute or chronic conditions causing inflammation, monitor infection or chronic inflammation, and help guide treatment decisions in conditions such as sepsis.
Infection Markers.summary: CRP is made by the liver in response to inflammation. Low levels are generally normal, while increased levels suggest inflammation in the body but do not identify the cause or location. Results must be interpreted with other tests, symptoms, and medical history. The standard CRP test is different from hs-CRP, which detects very small increases and is used to estimate heart disease risk.

Infection Markers.purpose: To measure the number of CD4 cells in blood, mainly to monitor immune system health in people with HIV, assess HIV disease progression and AIDS risk, and help monitor or diagnose other immune-related conditions such as after organ transplant, lymphoma, and DiGeorge syndrome.
Infection Markers.summary: A CD4 count reports the number of CD4 T lymphocytes in blood, which reflects immune system status. In people with HIV, falling CD4 counts suggest worsening immune suppression and a count of 200 cells per cubic millimeter or less indicates AIDS. Results are interpreted over time along with other clinical information, since normal ranges vary and high or low values can also occur with other conditions.

Infection Markers.purpose: Used with other tests to help diagnose and monitor conditions that cause inflammation, and to monitor an existing condition.
Infection Markers.summary: ESR measures how quickly red blood cells settle in a tube and is an indirect sign of inflammation. A high ESR suggests inflammation may be present, while a low ESR can be seen with certain blood disorders and other conditions. The test cannot diagnose a specific disease by itself and is often interpreted with other tests and clinical information.

Infection Markers.purpose: To help determine the cause of a pleural effusion by analyzing fluid removed from the pleural space, classifying it as transudate or exudate, and guiding further testing and diagnosis.
associated_symptoms: Chest pain that doesn't have another explanation
Dry cough that doesn't bring up mucus
Infection Markers.summary: Pleural fluid analysis evaluates abnormal fluid in the pleural space and commonly uses Light's criteria to distinguish transudate from exudate. Transudate is usually linked to pressure-related causes such as heart, kidney, or liver disease, while exudate is more often associated with inflammation, infection, cancer, or injury. Results help narrow the cause of pleural effusion and guide additional tests and treatment.

Infection Markers.purpose: Measures procalcitonin in blood to help determine whether a serious systemic bacterial infection or sepsis is present, distinguish bacterial from viral infections, guide antibiotic treatment decisions, monitor treatment response, and assess sepsis severity; it may also help diagnose kidney infections in children with urinary tract infections.
associated_symptoms: Feeling like you can't get enough air
Infection Markers.summary: Very high procalcitonin levels suggest sepsis, severe sepsis or septic shock, or a serious systemic bacterial infection. Mild or moderate increases may reflect an early bacterial infection or some noninfectious conditions, while low or decreasing levels can indicate that bacterial treatment is working.

Hematology.purpose: To measure the number of CD4 cells in blood, mainly to monitor immune system health in people with HIV, assess HIV disease progression and AIDS risk, and help monitor or diagnose other immune-related conditions such as after organ transplant, lymphoma, and DiGeorge syndrome.
Hematology.summary: A CD4 count reports the number of CD4 T lymphocytes in blood, which reflects immune system status. In people with HIV, falling CD4 counts suggest worsening immune suppression and a count of 200 cells per cubic millimeter or less indicates AIDS. Results are interpreted over time along with other clinical information, since normal ranges vary and high or low values can also occur with other conditions.

Hematology.purpose: Measures the types and amounts of hemoglobin in the blood to look for abnormal hemoglobin and help diagnose anemia, sickle cell disease, and other hemoglobin disorders.
associated_symptoms: Painful swelling of the hands and feet
Hematology.summary: Hemoglobin electrophoresis separates and measures normal and abnormal hemoglobin types in a blood sample. Results that are too high or too low can indicate hemoglobin disorders such as thalassemia, sickle cell trait or disease, hemoglobin C disease, or hemoglobin S-C disease. Results are interpreted along with symptoms, medical history, and other blood tests, and a recent blood transfusion can affect the outcome.
