Hematology.purpose: Measures LDH in blood or other body fluids to check for tissue damage and help diagnose or monitor a wide range of conditions, including diseases affecting blood, liver, lungs, kidneys, heart, pancreas, brain and spinal cord, as well as some infections and cancers; it can also help monitor treatment response.
Hematology.summary: LDH is an enzyme found in many tissues; elevated levels usually suggest tissue damage from disease, infection, or injury, but results are not specific and must be interpreted with symptoms and other tests. Low levels are uncommon and usually not a health problem, though they can be seen with high vitamin C or E intake or rare LDH deficiency. If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test may help identify the tissue source of the damage.

Hematology.lab_test_title: Protein Electrophoresis by Immunofixation Blood Test
Hematology.purpose: This test measures and separates blood proteins to check whether protein levels are too high or too low, and to help detect, diagnose, or monitor conditions that affect protein levels, especially multiple myeloma and other diseases involving abnormal proteins.
associated_symptoms: Bone pain, especially in the back or ribs
Anemia (low level of red blood cells)
High levels of calcium in the blood (hypercalcemia)
Numbness, tingling, or pain in the face, arms, and/or legs
Hematology.summary: The test can show whether protein levels are normal or whether specific proteins are too high or too low. Abnormal results may point to a variety of conditions, and the test can also be used to monitor a known disorder and whether it is worsening or responding to treatment. Results should be interpreted together with symptoms, medical history, age, and other test results.

Vitamins/Nutrients.purpose: A blood test used with other tests to help diagnose Wilson disease and other conditions involving too much or too little copper, and to monitor abnormal copper levels and treatment response.
associated_symptoms: Urine that's a darker color than usual
A type of anemia, called hemolytic anemia
Swelling from fluid buildup in your belly, lower legs, or feet
Sudden jerky movements you can't control
Green, gold, or brown rings around your irises
Abnormally low levels of white blood cells called neutrophils
Tingling in your hands and feet
Hair that is colorless, thin, breaks easily, and becomes unusually tangled
related_diseases_or_conditions: Too much copper in the blood
Vitamins/Nutrients.summary: Ceruloplasmin is a copper-carrying protein made by the liver. Low levels may suggest problems using or obtaining copper, including Wilson disease, Menkes syndrome, severe liver disease, kidney disease, or copper deficiency, while high levels may be associated with inflammatory or other conditions. Results must be interpreted along with copper tests and the patient’s symptoms and history.

Vitamins/Nutrients.purpose: Measures ferritin in the blood to assess how much iron is stored in the body, help diagnose or rule out iron-related conditions, monitor chronic conditions that affect iron levels, check for low iron before symptoms develop in high-risk people, and follow response to treatment.
associated_symptoms: Joint pain, commonly in the knees or hands
Change in skin color, which may look gray, metallic, or bronze
Vitamins/Nutrients.summary: Ferritin reflects stored iron. Low ferritin usually suggests iron deficiency, including iron deficiency anemia, while high ferritin may indicate iron overload or other conditions such as inflammation, liver disease, cancer, obesity, alcohol use disorder, or hyperthyroidism. Abnormal results do not always mean disease, and some medicines can affect levels.

Vitamins/Nutrients.purpose: To measure iron-related substances in the blood to assess iron levels, help diagnose anemia and iron overload conditions, evaluate iron storage and liver disease, check for restless legs syndrome and adult Still disease, and monitor treatment for iron deficiency or excess iron.
Vitamins/Nutrients.summary: Iron tests include serum iron, transferrin, TIBC, and ferritin tests. Results that are too low may suggest iron deficiency, anemia, or thalassemia, while results that are too high may suggest hemochromatosis, lead poisoning, or liver disease. Results are interpreted with symptoms, medical history, age, and other blood tests, and can be affected by medicines and menstrual cycles.

Vitamins/Nutrients.purpose: To measure the level of one or more B vitamins in blood or urine when vitamin B deficiency is suspected, including evaluation of symptoms or conditions that raise the risk of deficiency; vitamin B12 and folate testing is also used for some types of anemia.
associated_symptoms: Cracks at the corners of the mouth
Vitamins/Nutrients.summary: The test reports the amount of each B vitamin measured in blood or urine. Low levels suggest deficiency and may require more testing to find the cause and treatment with supplements or, in some cases, intravenous vitamins. Normal results do not always rule out a problem, and interpretation can be affected by inflammation, medicines, and lab-specific reference ranges.

Vitamins/Nutrients.purpose: To measure vitamin D levels in the blood, usually to check for vitamin D deficiency or excess and to help evaluate bone or other health conditions related to abnormal vitamin D levels; active vitamin D testing may also be used to monitor kidney problems or help find the cause of abnormal calcium levels.
related_diseases_or_conditions: Children with low vitamin D intake
Vitamins/Nutrients.summary: The test is usually reported as total vitamin D, or sometimes as vitamin D2 and D3. Low results may indicate inadequate intake or sunlight exposure, malabsorption, kidney or liver disease, or medicines affecting vitamin D levels. High or toxic results usually suggest too much vitamin D from supplements and may cause serious harm to organs and blood vessels.

Vitamins/Nutrients.purpose: Measures the amount of vitamin E in blood to check for vitamin E deficiency or excess, especially in people with absorption disorders, premature babies, or those taking vitamin E supplements.
associated_symptoms: Loss of feeling in your arms and legs
Problems walking and controlling your body movements
Vitamins/Nutrients.summary: A vitamin E test helps determine whether blood vitamin E levels are normal for age. Low levels suggest inadequate intake or absorption and may be treated with supplements and treatment of the underlying cause. High levels usually reflect too much supplementation and may increase bleeding risk, so supplements may need to be stopped.

Cardiovascular.purpose: To measure cholesterol and triglyceride levels in the blood, estimate risk for heart disease and related cardiovascular problems, and help guide steps to lower high cholesterol.
Cardiovascular.summary: This blood test measures total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides. Low LDL and high HDL are generally better for heart health, while high LDL and triglycerides can increase the risk of plaque buildup in arteries and future cardiovascular disease. Results may be calculated or directly measured, and healthy targets depend on age and other risk factors.

Cardiovascular.purpose: A blood test used mainly to help diagnose and monitor skeletal muscle injury and disease that cause elevated CK levels. It may also help evaluate damage to heart muscle or brain tissue, and in some cases help assess heart attack or stroke severity.
Cardiovascular.summary: CK is an enzyme found mostly in skeletal muscle, with smaller amounts in the heart and brain. Higher-than-normal CK usually suggests tissue damage, especially muscle damage, but the result does not identify the source or cause; CK isoenzyme testing and other tests may be needed to determine whether the elevation comes from skeletal muscle, heart, or brain.

Cardiovascular.purpose: Measures the amount of homocysteine in blood. It is used most often to assess vitamin B6, vitamin B12, and folic acid (folate) levels, help diagnose homocystinuria, and help understand risk for heart attack or stroke in people already at increased risk.
associated_symptoms: changes in the color of your skin or fingernails
sores on your tongue or in your mouth
tingling in your hands, feet, arms, and/or legs
numbness in your hands, feet, arms, and/or legs
Cardiovascular.summary: Low homocysteine is normal. High levels may suggest inadequate vitamin B6, B12, or folate intake, homocystinuria, or increased risk for cardiovascular and blood vessel disease. Results can also be influenced by age, sex, and smoking, and elevated values do not always mean a condition requiring treatment.

Cardiovascular.purpose: Measures LDH in blood or other body fluids to check for tissue damage and help diagnose or monitor a wide range of conditions, including diseases affecting blood, liver, lungs, kidneys, heart, pancreas, brain and spinal cord, as well as some infections and cancers; it can also help monitor treatment response.
Cardiovascular.summary: LDH is an enzyme found in many tissues; elevated levels usually suggest tissue damage from disease, infection, or injury, but results are not specific and must be interpreted with symptoms and other tests. Low levels are uncommon and usually not a health problem, though they can be seen with high vitamin C or E intake or rare LDH deficiency. If LDH is high, an LDH isoenzyme test may help identify the tissue source of the damage.

Cardiovascular.purpose: To measure lipoprotein(a) in the blood and help assess the risk of heart disease, stroke, and other blood vessel diseases, especially in people who may be at higher cardiovascular risk or have a family history of elevated lipoprotein(a).
Cardiovascular.summary: A high lipoprotein(a) level may indicate increased risk for heart and blood vessel disease, even when routine cholesterol results are normal. Lipoprotein(a) levels are largely determined by genes, usually stay fairly constant over time, and diet and exercise may not significantly change them.

Cardiovascular.purpose: Blood tests used mainly to help diagnose or rule out heart failure in people with symptoms, and sometimes to assess how serious heart failure is, predict worsening, check symptom changes, or monitor heart health after a heart attack or in certain acute heart conditions.
associated_symptoms: Swelling in the veins in your neck
Needing to urinate a lot, especially at night
Cardiovascular.summary: BNP and NT-proBNP are proteins released by the heart when it is working harder than normal. Normal results usually make heart failure unlikely, while higher-than-normal levels may suggest heart failure, though other conditions can also raise them. Results are interpreted with age, sex, medical history, and other tests.

Cardiovascular.purpose: Measures troponin in blood to help diagnose and monitor heart muscle damage, especially heart attack, unstable angina, and possible heart injury after surgery.
associated_symptoms: discomfort in the center or left side of the chest
Pain or discomfort in one or both arms
pain or discomfort in your back
trouble breathing when doing light physical activity
Feeling unusually tired for no reason
Sweating a lot for no reason
Cardiovascular.summary: Troponin is a heart muscle protein that normally stays very low in blood. Rising or high troponin levels indicate heart muscle injury, often from a heart attack, but they can also occur with other heart- or body-related conditions. Serial testing helps show whether levels are rising and how much damage may have occurred.

Coagulation.purpose: Used to check one or more clotting factors to see whether a person has too much, too little, or a missing/nonworking clotting factor, and to help evaluate bleeding or clotting problems in people with known factor disorders or who take blood thinners.
associated_symptoms: Heavy bleeding that doesn't stop with pressure after an injury, dental procedure, or surgery
Frequent nosebleeds that start on their own
Tiny red or brown spots under the skin
Pain in your arms or legs
Coagulation.summary: Lower than normal or missing clotting factors may indicate a bleeding disorder, while higher than normal levels may suggest a condition that causes excessive clotting. Results may help identify the type and severity of the problem, but additional tests are often needed to find the cause.

Coagulation.purpose: Measures the levels and/or activity of complement system proteins, either individually (such as C3 and C4) or as total complement activity (CH50/CH100), to help diagnose or monitor autoimmune diseases and sometimes certain infections.
Coagulation.summary: Low complement levels or activity may suggest the body is attacking its own tissues or clearing foreign substances, and can be seen in autoimmune disease, liver disease, kidney disease, hereditary angioedema, malnutrition, or recurrent infection. High levels may indicate acute or chronic inflammation, certain cancers, or ulcerative colitis, and in someone being treated for an autoimmune disease may mean treatment is working.

Coagulation.purpose: Used to check whether you may have a blood clot and whether more testing is needed for a clotting disorder; also used to monitor treatment for a clotting disorder such as disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
associated_symptoms: redness or darkening of the skin on the leg
Coagulation.summary: Low or normal D-dimer levels usually mean a clotting disorder is unlikely, while higher-than-normal levels may suggest a clot but are not specific. Results must be interpreted with symptoms, medical history, and other tests, since blood thinners can cause a false negative and many non-clotting conditions can raise D-dimer levels.

Coagulation.purpose: A PTT test measures how long it takes blood to clot and evaluates a specific group of clotting factors. It is used to find the cause of bleeding or bruising, investigate clotting problems, monitor heparin therapy, and assess bleeding risk before surgery or procedures.
Coagulation.summary: PTT results are reported in seconds and help show whether blood is clotting too slowly or too quickly. A prolonged PTT may suggest liver disease, vitamin K lack, inherited bleeding disorders, heparin excess, certain leukemias, or autoimmune conditions; a shortened PTT may be seen in early DIC or advanced cancers. Results are often interpreted together with a prothrombin time (PT) test.

Coagulation.purpose: Used to measure the number of platelets in the blood and/or assess how well platelets function to help diagnose or monitor problems with bleeding or clotting, evaluate platelet disorders, check bleeding risk before or during surgery, and monitor the effects of blood-thinning medicines.
associated_symptoms: Bleeding for a long time after a minor cut or injury
Pinpoint sized red spots on the skin
Purplish, red, or brown spots on your skin
Menstrual periods that last a long time
Pain, swelling, and warmth in your lower legs
related_diseases_or_conditions: Infection or damage to the bone marrow
Coagulation.summary: Platelet tests help determine whether platelet number or function is abnormal. Low platelet counts can cause excessive bleeding, while high counts can increase clotting risk; abnormal function tests may suggest inherited or acquired platelet disorders, and results are interpreted along with symptoms, history, and other blood tests.

Coagulation.lab_test_title: Protein C and Protein S Tests
Coagulation.purpose: These tests measure the amount and activity of protein C and protein S in the blood to help find the cause of unexplained blood clots, assess risk for future clots, check for protein C or S deficiency, determine whether the deficiency is due to low levels or dysfunctional proteins, and monitor changes in levels over time.
associated_symptoms: a blood clot before the age of 50 without a known reason
a blood clot in an unusual location, such as in the veins of the kidneys, liver, or brain
related_diseases_or_conditions: inherited protein C or S deficiency
Coagulation.summary: Lower-than-normal protein C or protein S levels, or proteins that do not work properly, indicate an increased risk of blood clots. Higher-than-normal levels are not known to cause health problems. If an inherited deficiency is suspected, genetic testing may be needed; acquired deficiencies may be temporary or long-lasting, and treatment can help reduce clot risk.

Coagulation.purpose: Measures how long it takes blood to clot and uses INR to standardize results across labs or methods. It is used to monitor warfarin therapy, evaluate abnormal bleeding or blood clots, check clotting before surgery or procedures, and help assess liver problems and vitamin K deficiency.
associated_symptoms: redness or darkening of the skin on the leg
Coagulation.summary: PT/INR results show whether blood is clotting too quickly or too slowly. A low INR or short PT may suggest increased clotting risk, while a high INR or long PT may suggest bleeding risk. Results are especially important for adjusting warfarin dose and are interpreted with symptoms, medical history, and other tests.

Others.purpose: Used to check for diseases of the central nervous system, and often to help diagnose multiple sclerosis (MS).
associated_symptoms: Tingling, numbness, or pain in the arms, legs, body, or face
Others.summary: A CSF IgG index measures IgG in cerebrospinal fluid. Higher-than-normal levels may suggest infection or an inflammatory or autoimmune condition affecting the central nervous system, while lower-than-normal levels may indicate the body is not making enough IgG antibodies.

Others.purpose: To help determine the cause of a pleural effusion by analyzing fluid removed from the pleural space, classifying it as transudate or exudate, and guiding further testing and diagnosis.
associated_symptoms: Chest pain that doesn't have another explanation
Dry cough that doesn't bring up mucus
Others.summary: Pleural fluid analysis evaluates abnormal fluid in the pleural space and commonly uses Light's criteria to distinguish transudate from exudate. Transudate is usually linked to pressure-related causes such as heart, kidney, or liver disease, while exudate is more often associated with inflammation, infection, cancer, or injury. Results help narrow the cause of pleural effusion and guide additional tests and treatment.

Others.purpose: Measures the total amount of protein in the blood and compares albumin to globulin. It is used as part of a comprehensive metabolic panel and may help diagnose or monitor kidney disease, liver disease, and nutritional problems, as well as assess liver and kidney function and overall protein/nutrient status.
Others.summary: This test evaluates total blood protein and the albumin/globulin ratio. Abnormal results can suggest liver, kidney, nutritional, immune, inflammatory, blood cancer, or other systemic conditions; interpretation depends on symptoms, medical history, and other blood tests.

Blood Bank/Transfusion.purpose: To check for red blood cell (RBC) antibodies before a blood transfusion or during pregnancy, so donor blood can be matched appropriately and pregnancy can be monitored for antibodies that may harm the fetus.
Blood Bank/Transfusion.summary: An RBC antibody screen looks for antibodies against foreign red blood cell antigens. A positive result means RBC antibodies are present and may affect transfusion compatibility or pregnancy, sometimes requiring further testing and closer monitoring. A negative result means no RBC antibodies were found, though antibodies can persist even if they are too few to detect.
